D. These are pregnancy pigment changes that fade after birth

Answer: D. These are pregnancy pigment changes that fade after birth

Pigmentation changes such as linea nigra, chloasma or melasma and darkened areolae are presumptive signs of pregnancy, the P in the PREGNANT mnemonic. They are caused by increased estrogen and progesterone, which stimulate melanocyte activity. These changes usually fade after delivery, although they may not disappear completely. Advise sunscreen and sun avoidance to limit facial darkening. Memory aid: P for pigmentation leads the PREGNANT mnemonic.

A is wrong: These changes are hormonal and do not indicate vitamin deficiency.

B is wrong: Iron supplements do not cause skin hyperpigmentation of this pattern.

C is wrong: Linea nigra and chloasma are hormonal changes, not signs of liver disease.

223. A woman at 24 weeks reports an increase in thin, whitish vaginal discharge without itching or odor. Which advice should the nurse give?

A. Use an antifungal cream since this is likely candidiasis

B. Go to the hospital now for possible rupture of membranes

C. Bathe daily, wear cotton underwear and avoid douching

D. Douche daily with vinegar water to lessen the discharge

Answer: C. Bathe daily, wear cotton underwear and avoid douching

Increased vaginal discharge or leukorrhea, listed under D in the MIND mnemonic of common discomforts, is caused by high estrogen levels that increase cervical and vaginal secretions. Hygiene measures such as daily bathing, cotton underwear and avoiding douching are appropriate. Douching is contraindicated in pregnancy because it can introduce air or infection. The woman should report itching, foul odor or a change in color, which suggest infection.

A is wrong: Nonirritating whitish discharge without itching is expected and does not need antifungals.

B is wrong: Ruptured membranes cause watery fluid leakage, not thin whitish nonirritating discharge.

D is wrong: Douching is avoided in pregnancy because of the risk of infection and air embolism.

224. A woman at 32 weeks who sells vegetables in a public market for many hours a day has varicose veins on her legs. Which advice is best?

A. Cross the legs when seated to support the swollen leg veins

B. Elevate the legs often, avoid long standing, wear support hose

C. Use knee-high stockings with tight elastic bands at the top

D. Massage the veins firmly upward to push the blood back

Answer: B. Elevate the legs often, avoid long standing, wear support hose

Varicose veins, the V in the CALVE group of discomforts, result from the weight of the uterus on pelvic veins and from progesterone relaxing the vein walls. Elevating the legs, avoiding prolonged standing or sitting, and wearing support stockings improve venous return. Crossing the legs and tight knee-high bands impede circulation, and massaging varicosities may dislodge a clot. Tip: anything that restricts flow is wrong, anything that promotes return is right.

A is wrong: Crossing the legs compresses the veins and worsens venous return.

C is wrong: Tight elastic bands constrict circulation and worsen venous stasis.

D is wrong: Massaging varicose veins is avoided because it may dislodge a thrombus.

225. A woman at 28 weeks complains of bloating and flatulence. Which advice should the nurse give?

A. Take a laxative every day to keep the bowels empty

B. Drink carbonated soft drinks after meals to release the gas

C. Avoid gas-forming foods and chew food slowly and well

D. Lie flat on her back for an hour after every large meal

Answer: C. Avoid gas-forming foods and chew food slowly and well

Flatulence, one of the 3F discomforts, results from progesterone slowing gastrointestinal motility and from pressure of the enlarging uterus on the bowel. Avoiding gas-forming foods such as cabbage and beans, chewing food thoroughly, exercising and maintaining regular bowel habits help reduce gas. Carbonated drinks add gas, lying flat after meals worsens discomfort and heartburn, and routine laxatives are avoided in pregnancy. Tip: slow gut plus pressure explains most pregnancy GI discomforts.

A is wrong: Routine laxative use is avoided in pregnancy and may cause dependence or preterm cramping.

B is wrong: Carbonated drinks add more gas to the gastrointestinal tract.

D is wrong: Lying flat after meals worsens bloating and heartburn and risks supine hypotension.

226. A woman at 36 weeks at a Bulacan health center says she cannot sleep well at night. Which measure should the nurse recommend?

A. Sleeping flat on her back without any supporting pillows

B. A cup of strong coffee in the late afternoon for energy

C. A sleeping pill bought from the pharmacy every night

D. A warm bath, a calm routine, side-lying with pillows

Answer: D. A warm bath, a calm routine, side-lying with pillows

Insomnia, the I in the MIND mnemonic, is common late in pregnancy because of fetal movement, urinary frequency and difficulty finding a comfortable position. Nonpharmacologic measures such as a warm bath, warm milk, a relaxing bedtime routine and a side-lying position supported by pillows are recommended. Over the counter sedatives are avoided without medical advice, caffeine worsens sleeplessness, and the supine position can cause supine hypotension. Tip: comfort measures first, drugs only when prescribed.

A is wrong: The supine position compresses the vena cava and is uncomfortable late in pregnancy.

B is wrong: Caffeine late in the day worsens insomnia.

C is wrong: Hypnotics should not be self-medicated during pregnancy.

227. A woman at 20 weeks asks why the nurse advised her to limit fried and fatty foods. According to the handout, the reason is that fats

A. supply the protein needed for fetal growth

B. are difficult to digest during pregnancy

C. directly cause neural tube defects in the fetus

D. are needed only during the first trimester

Answer: B. are difficult to digest during pregnancy

The handout's nutritional requirements list decreased fats because they are difficult to digest, increased protein for fetal development, and changes in carbohydrate intake by trimester. Progesterone slows gastric emptying and relaxes the cardiac sphincter, so fatty meals worsen nausea, heartburn and fullness. Protein, not fat, is the key nutrient emphasized for fetal tissue growth. Memory aid: low fat, high protein for the pregnant client.

A is wrong: Protein comes mainly from meat, fish, eggs and legumes, not fats.

C is wrong: Neural tube defects are linked to folic acid deficiency, not dietary fat.

D is wrong: The handout recommends decreased fats throughout pregnancy, not only in one trimester.

228. Based on the handout's nutritional guide, how should a pregnant woman's carbohydrate intake be adjusted across the trimesters?

A. Increased in the first trimester, then decreased in the second and third

B. Removed from the diet entirely to prevent excess weight gain

C. Kept exactly the same from the first through the third trimester

D. Decreased in the first trimester, then increased in the second and third

Answer: A. Increased in the first trimester, then decreased in the second and third

The handout states that carbohydrates are increased in the first trimester and decreased in the second and third trimesters. A higher carbohydrate intake early helps manage nausea and supply energy, while limiting carbohydrates later helps control excess weight gain and blood sugar. Note that current guidelines advise a steady adequate carbohydrate intake with an extra 340 to 450 kcal daily in later trimesters, so the decrease means avoiding excess. For the exam, key to the handout pattern.

B is wrong: Carbohydrates are an essential energy source and are never eliminated in pregnancy.

C is wrong: The handout specifies a change by trimester, not a constant intake.

D is wrong: This reverses the handout pattern, which increases carbohydrates early and decreases them later.

229. At a prenatal visit in a Laguna rural health unit, the nurse wants the single best indicator of a pregnant woman's overall health and nutrition. According to the handout, the nurse should monitor

A. her hemoglobin once each trimester

B. her weight at every prenatal visit

C. her blood pressure once a month

D. her urine glucose at each visit

Answer: B. her weight at every prenatal visit

The handout identifies weight as the best index of health in pregnancy. Normal weight gain is about 1 pound per month in the first trimester and about 1 pound per week in the second and third, for a total of 25 to 30 pounds. Sudden gain may signal preeclampsia, while poor gain may signal inadequate nutrition or fetal growth restriction. Weighing at every visit using the same scale gives the most useful trend. Tip: weight is the simplest and best index.

A is wrong: Hemoglobin screens for anemia but is not the best overall index of health.

C is wrong: Blood pressure screens for hypertension but does not reflect overall nutrition.

D is wrong: Urine glucose screens for diabetes and is not the overall index of health.

230. A woman at 36 weeks comes for a prenatal checkup in a Bataan health center. Where should the nurse expect to palpate the uterine fundus?

A. At the level of the xiphoid process

B. At the level of the umbilicus

C. Just above the pubic symphysis

D. Midway between symphysis and umbilicus

Answer: A. At the level of the xiphoid process

According to the handout, the fundus is at the pubic symphysis at 12 weeks, at the umbilicus at 20 weeks and at the xiphoid process at 36 weeks. After 36 weeks, especially in a primigravida, the fundal height may drop as the fetal head descends into the pelvis, which is lightening. Fundal height in centimeters roughly equals weeks of gestation between 20 and 36 weeks. Memory aid: 12 symphysis, 20 umbilicus, 36 xiphoid.

B is wrong: The fundus is at the umbilicus at about 20 weeks.

C is wrong: The fundus is just above the symphysis at about 12 weeks.

D is wrong: Midway between symphysis and umbilicus corresponds to about 16 weeks.

231. Twelve hours after a normal vaginal birth at a lying-in clinic, the nurse palpates the uterus. Where should the fundus be found if involution is normal?

A. At about the umbilicus, firm and midline

B. At the xiphoid process, firm and midline

C. No longer palpable in the abdomen at all

D. Just above the symphysis pubis, firm

Answer: A. At about the umbilicus, firm and midline

The handout states that within 24 hours postpartum the fundus is at the level of the umbilicus. Afterwards it descends about 1 to 2 cm or one fingerbreadth per day and is usually no longer palpable abdominally by about 10 days, with full involution in about 6 weeks. A fundus that is above the umbilicus, deviated or boggy suggests a full bladder or uterine atony. Tip: firm, midline and at the umbilicus on day 1 is the normal picture.

B is wrong: The fundus is at the xiphoid at 36 weeks of pregnancy, not after birth.

C is wrong: The uterus remains palpable in the abdomen for about the first 10 days.

D is wrong: The fundus reaches just above the symphysis only after several days of involution.

232. During the fourth Leopold's maneuver, the nurse faces the client's feet and slides the fingers down both sides of the lower abdomen toward the pelvic inlet. Based on the handout, this maneuver assesses

A. the location of the fetal back and small parts

B. the frequency and strength of uterine contractions

C. the fetal part that occupies the uterine fundus

D. fetal attitude, the degree of flexion of the head

Answer: D. fetal attitude, the degree of flexion of the head

In the handout, the first Leopold's maneuver identifies the fetal part in the fundus, the second locates the fetal back, the third checks engagement of the presenting part, and the fourth determines fetal attitude. In the fourth maneuver the nurse faces the woman's feet and palpates for the cephalic prominence to see whether the head is flexed. The client should void first and lie supine. Memory aid: Part, Back, Engagement, Attitude for maneuvers one to four.

A is wrong: The fetal back is located by the second maneuver.

B is wrong: Leopold's maneuvers assess fetal position and are not used to assess contractions.

C is wrong: The fetal part in the fundus is assessed by the first maneuver.

233. During assessment, the nurse notes that the long axis of the fetus is parallel to the long axis of the mother. Which term describes this relationship?

A. Fetal attitude

B. Fetal station

C. Fetal position

D. Fetal lie

Answer: D. Fetal lie

Fetal lie is the relationship between the long axis of the fetal body and the long axis of the mother. A parallel relationship is a longitudinal lie, which allows a cephalic or breech presentation, while a perpendicular one is a transverse lie, often requiring cesarean birth. Position relates the presenting part to the maternal pelvis quadrants, attitude is the degree of flexion, and station is the level relative to the ischial spines. Tip: lie is about axes, position is about quadrants.

A is wrong: Fetal attitude describes the degree of flexion or extension of the fetal body.

B is wrong: Station describes the level of the presenting part relative to the ischial spines.

C is wrong: Fetal position relates the presenting part to a quadrant of the maternal pelvis.

234. A nurse at a Cavite hospital documents LOA after a vaginal examination. This term describes fetal position, which the handout defines as the

A. relationship of the fetal long axis to the maternal axis

B. level of the presenting part in relation to ischial spines

C. relation of the presenting part to a quadrant of the pelvis

D. degree of flexion or extension of the fetal head and body

Answer: C. relation of the presenting part to a quadrant of the pelvis

Fetal position is the relationship of the presenting part to a specific quadrant of the maternal pelvis. It is written with three letters such as LOA, meaning left occiput anterior, where the occiput faces the left anterior quadrant. LOA and ROA are the most common and favorable positions for vaginal birth. Attitude describes flexion, lie describes the axes and station describes the level relative to the ischial spines. Tip: position uses letters, station uses numbers.

A is wrong: The relationship of the long axes describes fetal lie.

B is wrong: The level relative to the ischial spines describes fetal station.

D is wrong: The degree of flexion or extension describes fetal attitude.

235. On vaginal examination, the nurse palpates the fetal chin and mouth, and the fetal head and neck are hyperextended. Which attitude does this describe?

A. Face, which presents the widest diameter

B. Brow, which shows full flexion of the head

C. Vertex, which presents the smallest diameter

D. Military, in which the head is sharply flexed

Answer: A. Face, which presents the widest diameter

In the handout, fetal attitudes range from full flexion to full extension. Vertex or occiput is full flexion and presents the smallest diameter. Sinciput or military means the head is partially flexed or not flexed, brow is partial extension, and face means the head and neck are hyperextended, presenting the widest diameter. Face and brow presentations often lead to prolonged labor or cesarean birth. Memory aid: the more the head extends, the wider the diameter.

B is wrong: Brow presentation is partial extension, not full flexion.

C is wrong: Vertex is full flexion of the head, not hyperextension.

D is wrong: Military attitude means the head is partially flexed or not flexed, not sharply flexed.

236. The nurse reviews fetal attitudes with nursing students. Which statement correctly describes the sinciput or military attitude?

A. The head and neck are fully hyperextended

B. The head is partially extended toward the brow

C. The head is sharply flexed with chin on chest

D. The head is partially flexed or not flexed

Answer: D. The head is partially flexed or not flexed

The handout describes the sinciput or military attitude as one in which the head is partially flexed or not flexed, like a soldier standing at attention. Full flexion with the chin on the chest is the vertex or occiput attitude, partial extension is brow, and full hyperextension is face. The military attitude presents a larger diameter than the vertex, so labor may progress more slowly. Order to remember: vertex, military, brow, face, from most flexed to most extended.

A is wrong: Full hyperextension of the head and neck describes the face attitude.

B is wrong: Partial extension describes the brow attitude.

C is wrong: Sharp flexion with the chin on the chest describes the vertex attitude.

237. Which of the 4 P's of labor refers to the uterine contractions and maternal bearing down efforts that move the fetus through the pelvis?

A. Passageway

B. Passenger

C. Power

D. Psyche

Answer: C. Power

The 4 P's of labor are the passenger, the passageway, the power and the psyche. Power is the force of labor, which includes involuntary uterine contractions and the voluntary bearing down of the mother in the second stage. The passenger is the fetus, the passageway is the maternal pelvis with the gynecoid type being most favorable, and the psyche is the mother's emotional energy and anxiety level. Tip: power pushes, passenger moves, passageway receives, psyche influences all three.

A is wrong: The passageway refers to the maternal pelvis and soft tissues.

B is wrong: The passenger refers to the fetus, including size, position and presentation.

D is wrong: The psyche refers to the mother's emotional state and anxiety level.

238. An ultrasound at 39 weeks shows a large fetus in a breech presentation. Which of the 4 P's of labor is affected by these findings?

A. Passenger

B. Passageway

C. Psyche

D. Power

Answer: A. Passenger

The passenger refers to the fetus, and the handout lists its key factors as size, position and presentation. A large fetus or a noncephalic presentation such as breech can slow descent and complicate vaginal delivery. The cephalic presentation is the most favorable. The passageway is the maternal pelvis, the power is the force of contractions and the psyche is the emotional state of the mother. Tip: anything about the baby belongs to the passenger.

B is wrong: The passageway is the maternal pelvis, not the fetal size or presentation.

C is wrong: Psyche refers to maternal emotions and anxiety.

D is wrong: Power refers to uterine contractions and bearing down efforts.

239. A multigravida is in the second stage of labor at a Batangas lying-in clinic. Which description of her contractions and behavior matches the handout?

A. Every 3 to 5 minutes for 45 to 60 seconds, afraid of losing control

B. Every 15 minutes for 20 seconds, passive, sleepy and dependent

C. Every 10 minutes for 30 seconds, talkative and excited about the birth

D. Every 2 to 3 minutes, 60 to 90 seconds, irritable then participating

Answer: D. Every 2 to 3 minutes, 60 to 90 seconds, irritable then participating

The second stage lasts from full cervical dilatation to the birth of the baby. According to the handout, contractions occur every 2 to 3 minutes and last 60 to 90 seconds, and maternal behavior progresses from irritability to active participation as she begins to push. The talkative woman with contractions every 10 minutes is in the latent phase, and the fear of losing control fits the active phase. Crowning is the hallmark of the second stage.

A is wrong: These findings describe the active phase of the first stage.

B is wrong: Passive dependent behavior describes the taking-in phase after delivery, not the second stage.

C is wrong: These findings describe the latent phase of the first stage.

240. On the first postpartum day, a mother at a Marikina hospital asks the nurse to bring the baby to the nursery so she can sleep. Based on the handout, the nurse recognizes this as

A. a sign of postpartum depression that needs referral today

B. a failure of bonding that should be reported to social service

C. normal taking-in behavior, as refusing rooming-in can occur

D. letting-go behavior, showing she has accepted her new role

Answer: C. normal taking-in behavior, as refusing rooming-in can occur

Rubin's taking-in phase lasts about 1 to 3 days after delivery, when the mother is passive and dependent, focused on her own needs for rest, food and comfort, and reviews her labor experience. The handout notes that rejecting rooming-in is normal at this time. The nurse should meet her physical needs and still encourage short, supported contact with the baby. Current practice strongly promotes rooming-in and breastfeeding, so offer help rather than separation where possible.

A is wrong: A request for rest on day 1 is expected and is not by itself a sign of depression.

B is wrong: Fatigue on the first day does not indicate a failure of bonding.

D is wrong: The letting-go phase comes later, when she accepts the baby and her new role.

241. Two hours after delivery, the nurse checks a postpartum client's perineal pad and finds a stain of 1 to 2 inches. Based on the handout classification, this amount is

A. light or small, 10 to 25 mL

B. scant, about 10 mL

C. moderate, 25 to 50 mL

D. large or heavy, saturating in 1 hour

Answer: B. scant, about 10 mL

The handout classifies lochia on a perineal pad by stain size: 1 to 2 inches is scant at about 10 mL, about 4 inches is light or small at 10 to 25 mL, 4 to 6 inches is moderate at 25 to 50 mL, and a pad saturated within 1 hour is large or heavy. Accurate estimation helps detect postpartum hemorrhage early. Also check under the buttocks because blood may pool there. Memory aid: inches go up as the category goes up, 2, 4, 6, then soaked.

A is wrong: A light or small amount produces a stain of about 4 inches.

C is wrong: A moderate amount produces a stain of 4 to 6 inches.

D is wrong: A large or heavy amount saturates the pad within 1 hour.

242. A nurse at a Bacolod hospital notes that a postpartum client's perineal pad became fully saturated within 1 hour. How should this lochia be classified?

A. Light or small

B. Large or heavy

C. Scant

D. Moderate

Answer: B. Large or heavy

According to the handout, a pad saturated within 1 hour is classified as large or heavy lochia. Moderate lochia makes a 4 to 6 inch stain of 25 to 50 mL, light makes a 4 inch stain and scant a 1 to 2 inch stain. Heavy flow requires prompt assessment of the fundus for firmness and position, the bladder, and vital signs, because saturation within 30 to 60 minutes may indicate postpartum hemorrhage. Tip: one pad in one hour is heavy, act at once.

A is wrong: Light lochia makes only about a 4 inch stain.

C is wrong: Scant lochia makes only a 1 to 2 inch stain.

D is wrong: Moderate lochia makes a 4 to 6 inch stain and does not fully saturate the pad in an hour.

243. A primigravida at a Caloocan health center says she feels overwhelmed by the changes in her body and her life. The nurse understands that, according to the handout, pregnancy is best viewed as a

A. situational crisis due to a sudden event

B. maturational or developmental crisis

C. pathologic condition that needs treatment

D. adventitious crisis like a natural disaster

Answer: B. maturational or developmental crisis

The handout emphasizes that pregnancy is a maturational or developmental crisis, an expected life transition that requires new roles, coping and adjustment. It is not a disease, and most women adapt with support, education and anticipatory guidance. Situational crises arise from unexpected events such as job loss or illness, while adventitious crises come from disasters or violence. Exam tip: normal life transitions such as pregnancy, puberty and retirement are maturational crises.

A is wrong: A situational crisis results from an unexpected event, while pregnancy is an expected life stage.

C is wrong: Pregnancy is a normal physiologic process, not a pathologic condition.

D is wrong: Adventitious crises come from disasters or violence, not normal life transitions.

244. A woman at 33 weeks with a history of preterm labor asks why she should avoid intercourse for now. Which explanation is based on the handout?

A. Intercourse always ruptures the membranes in late pregnancy

B. Semen raises blood pressure and leads to preeclampsia

C. Orgasm may release prostaglandins that can trigger contractions

D. The pressure of intercourse directly causes placental abruption

Answer: C. Orgasm may release prostaglandins that can trigger contractions

The handout notes that orgasm may release prostaglandins, which can lead to uterine contractions. For a woman with a history of preterm labor this risk matters, so intercourse is restricted, while in a normal pregnancy it is safe unless there is bleeding. Other contraindications include repeated miscarriage, incompetent cervix, bleeding, placenta previa and premature rupture of membranes. Tip: think of anything that can start labor or bleeding early.

A is wrong: Intercourse does not routinely rupture the membranes in a normal pregnancy.

B is wrong: Semen does not cause hypertension or preeclampsia.

D is wrong: Intercourse is not a direct cause of placental abruption in the handout.

245. At a prenatal clinic in Pampanga, which client should the nurse advise to avoid sexual intercourse during pregnancy?

A. A woman at 26 weeks with occasional leg cramps at night

B. A woman at 20 weeks with an uncomplicated pregnancy and no bleeding

C. A woman at 14 weeks who has mild morning sickness on waking

D. A woman at 18 weeks with incompetent cervix and past miscarriages

Answer: D. A woman at 18 weeks with incompetent cervix and past miscarriages

The handout lists contraindications to intercourse in pregnancy: a history of repeated miscarriage, incompetent cervix, bleeding, preterm labor, placenta previa and premature rupture of membranes. A woman with an incompetent cervix and repeated losses is at risk because orgasm and prostaglandins may stimulate contractions and cervical change. In a normal pregnancy intercourse is safe, and the second trimester is often the most comfortable time. Tip: bleeding, cervix or labor risk means abstain.

A is wrong: Leg cramps are a common discomfort and not a contraindication.

B is wrong: Intercourse is safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy without bleeding.

C is wrong: Morning sickness is a common discomfort and not a contraindication.

246. During a prenatal visit, a woman says a few bottles of beer and some cigarettes during town fiestas are harmless. What is the best response by the nurse?

A. Tell her small amounts are safe once she is past the first trimester

B. Advise her to avoid smoking, alcohol and drugs all through pregnancy

C. Say alcohol is unsafe but light smoking is fine during pregnancy

D. Suggest switching to light beer and filtered cigarettes when at fiestas

Answer: B. Advise her to avoid smoking, alcohol and drugs all through pregnancy

The handout lists smoking, alcohol and drugs as things to avoid during pregnancy. Alcohol can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, and no safe amount or safe trimester has been established. Smoking causes vasoconstriction, low birth weight, preterm birth and placental problems, and illicit drugs carry teratogenic and withdrawal risks. The nurse should give clear advice and offer support for stopping. Tip: for pregnancy, the safe amount of alcohol and tobacco is zero.

A is wrong: No amount of alcohol has been shown to be safe in any trimester.

C is wrong: Smoking in any amount reduces placental blood flow and is not safe.

D is wrong: Light beer still contains alcohol and filtered cigarettes still harm the fetus.

247. A woman registers for prenatal care at a Quezon City health center. According to the handout, at least how many prenatal visits should she have during her pregnancy?

A. 3

B. 8

C. 12

D. 4

Answer: B. 8

The handout lists the needs of the pregnant woman as adequate prenatal visits of at least 8, tetanus toxoid immunization of at least 2 doses, and micronutrient supplementation with vitamin A and iron. This matches the DOH 1-2-5 schedule, which gives 1 visit in the first trimester, 2 in the second and 5 in the third, for a total of 8. Older DOH guidance required only 4 visits, and the WHO 2016 model now recommends 8 contacts. Tip: add 1 plus 2 plus 5 to get 8.

A is wrong: Three visits covers only the first two trimesters of the 1-2-5 schedule.

C is wrong: Twelve visits is more than the stated minimum of 8.

D is wrong: Four visits was the older minimum and is below the current handout standard.

248. A G1 at 20 weeks at a barangay health center has never received tetanus toxoid. According to the handout, at least how many TT doses should she receive to protect her and her newborn?

A. At least 2 doses

B. At least 3 doses

C. At least 5 doses

D. At least 1 dose

Answer: A. At least 2 doses

The handout lists at least 2 doses of tetanus toxoid as a need of the pregnant woman. TT1 is given as early as possible in pregnancy and gives no protection by itself, while TT2 is given at least 4 weeks later and provides about 80 percent protection for 3 years. Two doses therefore give the minimum protection against neonatal tetanus. The dose is 0.5 mL IM in the deltoid or buttocks. Tip: one dose primes, two doses protect.

B is wrong: Three doses extend protection but are not the minimum required.

C is wrong: Five doses give lifetime protection but are not the minimum for pregnancy.

D is wrong: One dose of TT gives no protection, so it is not enough.

249. A woman at a Rizal health center has received her fourth dose of tetanus toxoid. How should the nurse describe her protection?

A. About 99 percent protection for 10 years

B. About 99 percent protection for her lifetime

C. About 80 percent protection for 3 years

D. About 90 percent protection for 5 years

Answer: A. About 99 percent protection for 10 years

Per the handout schedule, TT4 is given at least 1 year after TT3 and gives about 99 percent protection for 10 years. TT2 gives about 80 percent for 3 years, TT3 about 90 percent for 5 years, and TT5 given at least 1 year after TT4 gives lifetime protection. All doses are 0.5 mL intramuscular in the right or left deltoid or the buttocks. Memory aid for duration: none, 3, 5, 10, lifetime for TT1 to TT5.

B is wrong: Lifetime protection is achieved only after TT5.

C is wrong: About 80 percent for 3 years is the protection from TT2.

D is wrong: About 90 percent for 5 years is the protection from TT3.

250. A nurse at a Pasay health center dispenses iron supplements to a pregnant woman. According to the handout, what is the correct dose and schedule?

A. A 120 mg iron tablet once a week after meals

B. A 10,000 IU tablet twice a week from the 4th month

C. A 60 mg iron and 400 mcg folic acid tablet once daily

D. A 60 mg iron and 400 mcg folic acid tablet twice a week

Answer: C. A 60 mg iron and 400 mcg folic acid tablet once daily

The handout lists iron as a 60 mg iron with 400 mcg folic acid tablet taken daily throughout pregnancy to prevent anemia. Vitamin A 10,000 IU twice a week starting on the 4th month is the other DOH micronutrient. Micronutrient supplements are prescribed to prevent anemia, vitamin A deficiency and other nutritional disorders. Iron is best absorbed with vitamin C and may cause dark stools and constipation. Tip: iron is daily, vitamin A is twice weekly.

A is wrong: A weekly 120 mg dose does not match the handout schedule.

B is wrong: 10,000 IU twice a week from the 4th month is the vitamin A schedule.

D is wrong: The handout schedule for iron with folic acid is daily, not twice weekly.

251. A woman at 22 weeks asks which prenatal supplement she takes at 600 to 2000 IU daily to help absorb calcium. The nurse identifies this as

A. Iodine

B. Vitamin D

C. Vitamin A

D. Folic acid

Answer: B. Vitamin D

According to the handout table of prenatal drugs, vitamin D is given at 600 to 2000 IU per day for calcium absorption and bone health. Calcium is given at 1000 to 1300 mg per day, folic acid at 400 to 800 mcg per day to prevent neural tube defects, iron at 60 mg to prevent anemia and iodine at 150 mcg per day for thyroid function and fetal brain development. Vitamin D and calcium work together for fetal bones and teeth. Tip: D for density of bones.

A is wrong: Iodine is given at 150 mcg per day for thyroid and brain development.

C is wrong: Vitamin A is given at 10,000 IU twice a week from the 4th month.

D is wrong: Folic acid is given at 400 to 800 mcg per day to prevent neural tube defects.

252. A 53-year-old menopausal woman at a barangay health center asks the nurse which nutrient she should increase in her diet. The best answer is

A. Calcium

B. Sodium

C. Folic acid

D. Iron

Answer: A. Calcium

The handout reminds nurses that calcium needs to be increased in the diet of a menopausal client. After menopause the drop in estrogen speeds bone resorption and raises the risk of osteoporosis and fractures. Dietary sources include milk, cheese, small fish eaten with bones such as dilis, and green leafy vegetables, with vitamin D to aid absorption and weight bearing exercise. Iron needs actually fall after menses stop. Tip: menopause plus bones equals calcium.

B is wrong: Sodium should be limited, not increased, to protect blood pressure.

C is wrong: Folic acid is emphasized before and during pregnancy, not for menopause.

D is wrong: Iron needs decrease after menopause because menstrual losses stop.

253. A woman with epilepsy at a Cebu clinic plans to become pregnant. Which drug on her medication list should the nurse flag as a common teratogen listed in the handout?

A. Valproate

B. Ferrous sulfate

C. Paracetamol

D. Folic acid

Answer: A. Valproate

The handout lists common teratogenic drugs: isotretinoin, thalidomide, warfarin, methotrexate, valproate, lithium, tetracyclines, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, retinoids and anticancer drugs. Valproate is strongly linked to neural tube defects and developmental problems, so a woman planning pregnancy should have her antiseizure regimen reviewed by the physician before conception, never stopped abruptly. Paracetamol, iron and folic acid are considered safe. Tip: remember the list as drugs that need preconception review.

B is wrong: Ferrous sulfate is a routine prenatal supplement to prevent anemia.

C is wrong: Paracetamol is the preferred analgesic and antipyretic in pregnancy.

D is wrong: Folic acid is recommended to prevent neural tube defects, not a teratogen.

254. A woman at 7 weeks with chronic hypertension at a Davao clinic is taking an ACE inhibitor. What is the nurse's best action?

A. Tell her to stop all her medicines at home right away

B. Continue the drug since all antihypertensives are safe

C. Double the dose to keep her blood pressure well controlled

D. Notify the physician, since ACE inhibitors are teratogenic

Answer: D. Notify the physician, since ACE inhibitors are teratogenic

ACE inhibitors and ARBs are on the handout list of common teratogenic drugs, as they can cause fetal kidney damage, oligohydramnios and skull defects. The nurse should notify the physician promptly so that the drug can be changed to one considered safer in pregnancy, such as methyldopa or labetalol. The woman should not stop her medicines abruptly on her own, because uncontrolled hypertension is also dangerous. Tip: notify the prescriber rather than stop or adjust a drug yourself.

A is wrong: Stopping all medicines abruptly can cause dangerous rebound hypertension.

B is wrong: Not all antihypertensives are safe, and ACE inhibitors are known teratogens.

C is wrong: Increasing the dose increases fetal exposure to a teratogen.

255. During a family planning session in a barangay health center, the nurse cites the handout figure for the average number of members in a Filipino family. What is this figure?

A. 4 to 5 members

B. 8 to 10 members

C. 2 to 3 members

D. 6 to 7 members

Answer: A. 4 to 5 members

The handout section on the RH Law, RA 10354, notes an average of 4 to 5 family members together with a recommended birth spacing of 1 child every 3 years. These figures support responsible parenthood, which means planning family size and spacing births so that parents can meet their children's needs. The law guarantees universal access to information and services for family planning and maternal health. Tip: link RA 10354 with 4 to 5 members and 3 year spacing.

B is wrong: Eight to ten members is far larger than the handout average.

C is wrong: Two to three members is smaller than the handout average.

D is wrong: Six to seven members is larger than the handout average.

256. At her first prenatal visit, a woman asks why her blood type and Rh factor are being tested. The nurse explains that this test identifies the risk of

A. iron deficiency anemia or a hidden infection

B. urinary tract infection and kidney problems

C. gestational diabetes later in the pregnancy

D. Rh incompatibility between her and the fetus

Answer: D. Rh incompatibility between her and the fetus

Blood typing and Rh factor determination are routine prenatal tests that identify Rh incompatibility. An Rh negative mother carrying an Rh positive fetus may form antibodies that attack fetal red cells in a later pregnancy, causing hemolytic disease of the newborn. Rh immune globulin is given at about 28 weeks and within 72 hours after delivery to prevent sensitization. Other tests target other problems: CBC for anemia and infection, FBS for diabetes and urinalysis for UTI.

A is wrong: Anemia and infection are screened by the complete blood count.

B is wrong: UTI and kidney problems are screened by urinalysis.

C is wrong: Gestational diabetes risk is screened by fasting blood sugar or glucose tolerance testing.

257. A woman at 10 weeks provides a urine sample at a rural health unit. According to the handout, routine prenatal urinalysis screens for

A. anemia, infection and problems with blood clotting

B. UTI, kidney issues, protein and sugar in urine

C. syphilis and other sexually transmitted infections

D. the father of the baby through fetal DNA in urine

Answer: B. UTI, kidney issues, protein and sugar in urine

The handout states that urinalysis screens for urinary tract infection, kidney issues, and protein and sugar in the urine. Protein may signal preeclampsia or renal disease, while glucose may suggest gestational diabetes. The CBC checks for anemia, infection and clotting problems, VDRL or RPR screens for syphilis, and the noninvasive prenatal paternity test uses maternal blood. A clean catch midstream specimen gives the most accurate result.

A is wrong: Anemia, infection and clotting problems are checked by the CBC.

C is wrong: Syphilis is screened by VDRL or RPR blood tests.

D is wrong: Paternity testing uses maternal blood, not routine urinalysis.

258. A nurse explains the prenatal laboratory tests ordered for a woman at 9 weeks. Which pairing of test and reason is correct according to the handout?

A. Urinalysis, to identify Rh incompatibility early

B. Hepatitis B screening, to detect gestational diabetes

C. Fasting blood sugar, to check for anemia and infection

D. Complete blood count, for anemia, infection and clotting

Answer: D. Complete blood count, for anemia, infection and clotting

According to the handout, the complete blood count checks for anemia, infection and clotting issues. Fasting blood sugar assesses the risk of gestational diabetes, HBsAg detects hepatitis B infection, blood typing and Rh factor identify Rh incompatibility, and urinalysis screens for UTI, kidney problems, protein and sugar. The HIV test is required under RA 11166 for early management and VDRL or RPR screens for syphilis. Tip: match each test to the system it checks.

A is wrong: Rh incompatibility is identified by blood typing and Rh factor, not urinalysis.

B is wrong: HBsAg screening detects hepatitis B infection, not diabetes.

C is wrong: Fasting blood sugar screens for gestational diabetes, not anemia.

259. A woman at 7 weeks is scheduled for an ultrasound to confirm an early pregnancy. Which type is typically used in this early stage, according to the handout?

A. Transvaginal ultrasound

B. 4-D or dynamic 3-D ultrasound

C. Advanced targeted ultrasound

D. Fetal echocardiography

Answer: A. Transvaginal ultrasound

The handout states that transvaginal ultrasound is used during the early stages of pregnancy, because the probe is closer to the small uterus and gives clearer images. A standard ultrasound gives 2D images, an advanced ultrasound targets a specific problem, Doppler detects the heartbeat at about 10 to 12 weeks, 3-D gives three dimensional images, and 4-D shows the face and movements. The client does not need a full bladder for a transvaginal scan. Tip: early equals transvaginal.

B is wrong: 4-D ultrasound is used to look at the face and movements later in pregnancy.

C is wrong: An advanced ultrasound is used to target a specific suspected problem.

D is wrong: Fetal echocardiography assesses congenital heart defects, not early pregnancy confirmation.

260. A woman at 22 weeks at a Manila hospital has a family history of congenital heart disease. Which test should the nurse expect to be ordered to assess the fetal heart?

A. Glucose tolerance test

B. Transvaginal ultrasound

C. Fetal echocardiography

D. Non-invasive paternity test

Answer: C. Fetal echocardiography

The handout lists fetal echocardiography as the ultrasound used to assess congenital heart defects. It provides a detailed view of the fetal heart structure and blood flow and is usually done in the second trimester. Transvaginal ultrasound is used in early pregnancy, the noninvasive prenatal paternity test determines the father, and the glucose tolerance test identifies gestational diabetes. Tip: echo equals heart, whether in the adult or in the fetus.

A is wrong: The glucose tolerance test screens for gestational diabetes.

B is wrong: Transvaginal ultrasound is mainly used in early pregnancy, not for detailed heart study.

D is wrong: The paternity test identifies the father and does not assess the fetal heart.

261. A couple at a prenatal clinic asks which ultrasound will let them see their baby's face and movements before delivery. The nurse identifies the

A. Doppler ultrasound device

B. standard 2D ultrasound

C. transvaginal ultrasound

D. Dynamic 3-D or 4-D scan

Answer: D. Dynamic 3-D or 4-D scan

According to the handout, 4-D or dynamic 3-D ultrasound is used to look at the face and movements of the baby before delivery, because it adds real time motion to three dimensional images. A standard ultrasound gives 2D images, transvaginal ultrasound is used in early pregnancy, and Doppler detects the fetal heartbeat at about 10 to 12 weeks. 3-D alone gives still three dimensional images. Tip: the fourth dimension is time, so 4-D shows movement.

A is wrong: Doppler detects the heartbeat but does not show the face or movements.

B is wrong: A standard ultrasound gives flat 2D images, not moving three dimensional views.

C is wrong: Transvaginal ultrasound is used in early pregnancy and does not show the face in motion.

262. A pregnant woman at a Makati clinic wants to know who fathered her baby without risking the pregnancy. Which test from the handout serves this purpose?

A. Chorionic villus sampling

B. Non-invasive prenatal paternity test

C. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein

D. Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling

Answer: B. Non-invasive prenatal paternity test

The handout lists the non-invasive prenatal paternity test, or NIPP, as the test to determine the father of the child. It analyzes fetal DNA circulating in the mother's blood and compares it with the alleged father's sample, so there is no risk of miscarriage. Chorionic villus sampling and PUBS are invasive and used for chromosomal or blood studies, while MSAFP screens for neural tube defects and chromosomal problems. Tip: noninvasive means maternal blood draw only.

A is wrong: Chorionic villus sampling is invasive and used for chromosomal abnormalities.

C is wrong: MSAFP screens for neural tube defects and chromosomal disorders, not paternity.

D is wrong: PUBS is invasive and used mainly for fetal blood studies such as Rh incompatibility.

263. A woman at 30 weeks at a Pasig hospital is scheduled for a nonstress test. Which description is correct, based on the handout?

A. An invasive test that measures FHR response to induced contractions

B. An ultrasound done at 10 to 13 weeks that samples chorionic villi

C. Noninvasive test after 28 weeks of FHR response to fetal movement

D. A blood test done at 16 weeks that measures alpha-fetoprotein levels

Answer: C. Noninvasive test after 28 weeks of FHR response to fetal movement

The nonstress test is noninvasive, done after 28 weeks, and measures the fetal heart rate in response to fetal movement. A reactive result shows two accelerations of 15 bpm lasting 15 seconds within 20 minutes, indicating adequate fetal oxygenation. The contraction stress test correlates the FHR with uterine contractions induced by oxytocin or nipple stimulation. Alpha-fetoprotein is a maternal blood screen and CVS samples chorionic villi. Tip: NST is movement, CST is contractions.

A is wrong: Measuring FHR response to induced contractions describes the contraction stress test.

B is wrong: Sampling chorionic villi describes chorionic villus sampling.

D is wrong: Measuring alpha-fetoprotein is a maternal serum screening test, not the NST.

264. A woman at 16 weeks is scheduled for a triple screen test. The nurse explains that this test measures

A. glucose, insulin and hemoglobin A1c

B. lecithin, sphingomyelin and surfactant

C. estrogen, progesterone and prolactin

D. alpha-fetoprotein, hCG and estriol

Answer: D. alpha-fetoprotein, hCG and estriol

The handout describes the triple screen as measuring high and low levels of alpha-fetoprotein together with abnormal levels of hCG and estriol. The pattern helps estimate the risk of neural tube defects and chromosomal disorders such as Down syndrome. The quad screen adds inhibin A to assess probabilities of genetic disorders. Like MSAFP, it is a screening test, so abnormal results require diagnostic tests such as amniocentesis. Memory aid: triple equals AFP, hCG, estriol.

A is wrong: Glucose and related values are used for diabetes testing, not the triple screen.

B is wrong: The L/S ratio from amniotic fluid assesses fetal lung maturity.

C is wrong: Estrogen, progesterone and prolactin are not the components of the triple screen.

265. A woman at 17 weeks asks the nurse what the quad screen test is for. According to the handout, the quad screen is used to

A. assess the probability of possible genetic disorders

B. measure the fetal heart response to contractions

C. determine the father of the baby from fetal DNA

D. confirm the diagnosis of Down syndrome with certainty

Answer: A. assess the probability of possible genetic disorders

The handout describes the quad screen test as a way to assess the probabilities of potential genetic disorders. It measures AFP, hCG, estriol and inhibin A in maternal blood, usually between 15 and 20 weeks. Because it gives a risk estimate, an abnormal result is followed by diagnostic tests such as amniocentesis, which can confirm chromosomal problems. Tip: screening tests estimate probability, diagnostic tests confirm.

B is wrong: Fetal heart response to contractions is measured by the contraction stress test.

C is wrong: Paternity is determined by the noninvasive prenatal paternity test.

D is wrong: A screening test gives a probability and cannot confirm a diagnosis.

266. A woman at 16 weeks is told her MSAFP result is abnormal and cries, saying her baby surely has a birth defect. What is the best response by the nurse?

A. The result proves that the fetus has a neural tube defect

B. The test is unreliable, so she can ignore the abnormal result

C. The result means she should prepare for termination right away

D. It is only a screening test, and more tests are needed

Answer: D. It is only a screening test, and more tests are needed

The handout stresses that maternal alpha-fetoprotein is a screening test, not a diagnostic test. An abnormal value raises the probability of a problem, but results can be affected by wrong dating, multiple gestation or other factors. Diagnostic follow-up such as a detailed ultrasound or amniocentesis is needed to confirm. Remember that high AFP suggests neural tube defects and low AFP suggests Down syndrome. Tip: screening means suspicion, diagnosis means confirmation.

A is wrong: An abnormal screening result does not prove a defect without diagnostic testing.

B is wrong: The result should not be ignored because it needs follow-up testing.

C is wrong: No decision should be made on a screening result alone, and termination is not legal in the Philippines.

267. A woman at 16 weeks at a Quezon City hospital has a maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein level that is lower than expected. Which condition should the nurse anticipate being investigated?

A. Rh incompatibility

B. Neural tube defect

C. Down syndrome

D. Gestational diabetes

Answer: C. Down syndrome

According to the handout, low AFP is associated with Down syndrome, while high AFP is associated with neural tube defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly. A low result is followed by further screening and diagnostic tests such as amniocentesis for karyotyping. MSAFP remains a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Memory aid: Low AFP, Down goes low, while High AFP means an open neural tube lets protein leak high.

A is wrong: Rh incompatibility is identified by blood typing and Rh factor or PUBS.

B is wrong: Neural tube defects are linked to high, not low, AFP levels.

D is wrong: Gestational diabetes is screened by blood glucose testing, not AFP.

268. A fetus of an Rh negative mother at 24 weeks is suspected of having anemia. Which test from the handout samples fetal blood from the umbilical cord for this problem?

A. Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling

B. Amniocentesis with fetal karyotype study

C. Chorionic villus sampling

D. Biophysical profile

Answer: A. Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling

Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling, or PUBS, obtains fetal blood from the umbilical vein and is done after 17 weeks. The handout lists Rh incompatibility as its main indication, since it allows direct measurement of fetal hemoglobin and, if needed, intrauterine transfusion. Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid and CVS samples chorionic villi. Memory aid CAP: Chorionic villus sampling for chorion, Amniocentesis for amniotic fluid, PUBS for umbilical cord blood.

B is wrong: Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid for chromosomes, NTDs and lung maturity.

C is wrong: Chorionic villus sampling obtains placental tissue at 10 to 13 weeks for chromosomes.

D is wrong: A biophysical profile is noninvasive and does not obtain fetal blood.

269. A 38-year-old woman at 11 weeks wants the earliest available test to check for chromosomal abnormality. According to the handout, which test is done at 10 to 13 weeks?

A. Nonstress test

B. Chorionic villus sampling

C. Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling

D. Amniocentesis

Answer: B. Chorionic villus sampling

According to the handout, chorionic villus sampling is done at 10 to 13 weeks and samples the chorionic villi to detect chromosomal abnormality. It gives results earlier than amniocentesis, which is usually done at 14 to 20 weeks, and PUBS, which is done after 17 weeks. The nonstress test assesses fetal well being after 28 weeks and does not detect chromosomes. Tip: CVS comes first in time, matching the C that starts the CAP mnemonic.

A is wrong: The nonstress test evaluates fetal heart rate and not chromosomes.

C is wrong: PUBS is done after 17 weeks and is mainly for fetal blood studies.

D is wrong: Amniocentesis is done later, at about 14 to 20 weeks.

270. A few hours after amniocentesis at a Manila hospital, a woman reports mild cramping and slight soreness at the puncture site with no fever. How should the nurse interpret this?

A. These show the needle injured the fetus during the test

B. These indicate preterm labor that needs tocolysis now

C. These are expected minor side effects of the procedure

D. These are signs of placental abruption needing surgery

Answer: C. These are expected minor side effects of the procedure

The handout notes that side effects of amniocentesis may include cramping, slight fluid leak and minor irritation at the puncture site. Mild symptoms without fever are expected and are managed with rest and observation. The client should report persistent fluid leakage, bleeding, fever, chills, severe pain or regular contractions, which may signal infection, membrane rupture or labor. Ultrasound guidance makes fetal injury rare. Tip: mild and local is expected, severe or systemic needs reporting.

A is wrong: Mild cramping and soreness do not indicate fetal injury.

B is wrong: Mild cramping without regular contractions does not indicate preterm labor.

D is wrong: Placental abruption causes severe pain and bleeding, not mild cramps.

271. A woman at a Quezon City health center asks how long a Norplant progestin implant in her upper arm will prevent pregnancy. According to the handout, the nurse answers

A. 1 year

B. 3 months

C. 5 years

D. 10 years

Answer: C. 5 years

The handout describes Norplant as progestin capsules placed under the skin of the upper arm that provide contraception for 5 years. Its side effects are remembered as WHAM: weight gain, headache and hirsutism, acne and menstrual bleeding irregularities. Note that the original Norplant has been discontinued, and currently used implants are Jadelle for 5 years and Implanon or Nexplanon for 3 years. For the exam, key to the handout figure of 5 years.

A is wrong: One year is far shorter than the handout duration of Norplant.

B is wrong: Three months is the duration of an injectable such as DMPA, not an implant.

D is wrong: Ten years is longer than the handout duration and is closer to a copper IUD.

272. A woman has a progestin implant inserted in her upper arm at a family planning clinic. When does the handout say the implant becomes effective?

A. After her next three menstrual cycles

B. After 20 to 25 ejaculations of her partner

C. Only after 3 months of a backup method

D. Within 24 hours after insertion

Answer: D. Within 24 hours after insertion

The handout states that the Norplant implant is effective within 24 hours after insertion, and it provides protection for 5 years. In practice this applies when it is inserted during the first days of the menstrual cycle, otherwise a backup method is advised for 7 days. The 20 to 25 ejaculation rule applies to vasectomy, not implants. The client should be counseled on WHAM side effects. Tip: implant works by the next day, vasectomy needs 20 to 25 ejaculations.

A is wrong: Waiting for three cycles is not required for the implant to work.

B is wrong: The 20 to 25 ejaculation rule refers to vasectomy.

C is wrong: A 3 month backup period does not apply to the implant.

273. A nurse at a barangay health center teaches pregnant women about amniotic fluid. Which statement about its function is correct?

A. It transfers oxygen and nutrients between mother and fetus

B. It protects from temperature and pressure changes

C. It produces the hormones that maintain the pregnancy

D. It filters the fetal blood to remove waste products

Answer: B. It protects from temperature and pressure changes

The handout states that amniotic fluid protects the fetus from temperature and pressure changes and helps ensure adequate oxygenation, partly by preventing compression of the umbilical cord. It also allows fetal movement and lung development. Its main component is fetal urine, and the normal volume is 800 to 1,200 mL. Oxygen and nutrient transfer and waste filtration are functions of the placenta, which also produces hormones. Tip: fluid cushions, placenta exchanges.

A is wrong: Oxygen and nutrient transfer is the function of the placenta.

C is wrong: Hormones that maintain pregnancy are produced by the placenta.

D is wrong: Waste filtration for the fetus is done by the placenta.

Obstetric Nursing, Abnormal (261)

1. Infertility is defined as the inability of a couple to conceive after how long of frequent, unprotected sexual intercourse?

A. One year

B. Two years

C. Three months

D. Six months for every couple

Answer: A. One year

Infertility is the inability to conceive after ONE year of frequent, unprotected intercourse. Most fertile couples conceive within a year, so a shorter period would label too many normal couples as infertile. Evaluation may start after 6 months when the woman is older than 35. Memory aid: one year of trying means infertility work-up.

B is wrong: Two years would delay evaluation, the standard is one year.

C is wrong: Three months is too short, since many fertile couples need longer to conceive.

D is wrong: Six months is only an earlier cutoff used for women older than 35, not for every couple.

2. A 30-year-old woman who has tried to conceive for 14 months is being evaluated at a clinic in Quezon City. Among women, what is the most common cause of infertility?

A. Congenital absence of the uterus

B. Hostile cervical mucus

C. Blocked fallopian tubes from past infection

D. Problems with ovulation

Answer: D. Problems with ovulation

The most common cause of female infertility is a problem with ovulation, such as PCOS, thyroid disease, or hormonal imbalance. If no mature egg is released there is nothing to fertilize. Clues are irregular or absent menses. Evaluation includes basal body temperature, midluteal progesterone, and hormone tests. Tip: no ovulation equals no baby.

A is wrong: Uterine absence is rare and usually found in adolescence because of amenorrhea.

B is wrong: Cervical mucus factors are an uncommon cause of female infertility.

C is wrong: Tubal blockage is a recognized cause but is less common than ovulatory disorders.

3. A nurse explains the result of a semen analysis to a couple. What is the most common cause of infertility in males?

A. Retrograde ejaculation

B. Erectile dysfunction

C. Undescended testis in childhood

D. Low sperm count

Answer: D. Low sperm count

Low sperm count (oligospermia) is the most common cause of male infertility. Too few sperm lowers the chance that one will reach and fertilize the ovum. The semen analysis is the first test for the male partner, and the man should abstain from ejaculation for 2 to 5 days before collecting the specimen. Remember: male factor equals count, female factor equals ovulation.

A is wrong: Retrograde ejaculation is uncommon and usually follows surgery or diabetes.

B is wrong: Erectile dysfunction affects intercourse but is not the leading cause of male infertility.

C is wrong: Undescended testis is a risk factor but not the most common cause.

4. According to the review handout, a sperm count of what level is considered low and is the most common cause of male infertility?

A. Less than 60 million per mL

B. Less than 80 million per mL

C. Less than 20 million per mL

D. Less than 100 million per mL

Answer: C. Less than 20 million per mL

The handout lists a low sperm count as less than 20 million per mL, with a normal total count of greater than 39 million. Caveat: the current WHO lower reference limit for concentration is about 16 million per mL, and 39 million is the total count per ejaculate, so key to the handout number for the exam. Low counts reduce the chance of fertilization. Memory aid: twenty or less is low.

A is wrong: Sixty million per mL is above the handout cutoff for a low count.

B is wrong: Eighty million per mL is well above the handout cutoff.

D is wrong: One hundred million per mL is far above the handout cutoff.

5. A nurse reviews the semen analysis of a man at a fertility clinic in Makati. Which volume per ejaculation is within the normal range?

A. 0.2 to 1.0 mL

B. 10.0 to 15.0 mL

C. 8.0 to 12.0 mL

D. 1.5 to 7.6 mL

Answer: D. 1.5 to 7.6 mL

Normal semen volume per ejaculation is 1.5 to 7.6 mL. Very low volume may point to ejaculatory duct obstruction, retrograde ejaculation, or hormonal problems. Volume is one of five handout parameters, along with count, morphology, pH, and motility. Tip: the average ejaculate is about a teaspoon, roughly 2 to 5 mL.

A is wrong: A volume of 0.2 to 1.0 mL is low and may indicate obstruction or retrograde ejaculation.

B is wrong: A volume of 10.0 to 15.0 mL is abnormally high and not normal.

C is wrong: A volume of 8.0 to 12.0 mL is higher than the normal range.

6. The nurse teaches a couple that normal semen is slightly alkaline. Which pH range is normal for semen?

A. 5.5 to 6.5

B. 7.2 to 8.0

C. 4.0 to 5.0

D. 8.5 to 9.5

Answer: B. 7.2 to 8.0

Normal semen pH is 7.2 to 8.0. The alkaline fluid buffers the acidic vaginal environment so that sperm can survive and move toward the cervix. Semen that is too acidic or too alkaline lowers sperm viability and may signal infection or duct obstruction. Memory aid: semen is slightly alkaline, vagina is acidic.

A is wrong: A pH of 5.5 to 6.5 is acidic and too low for normal semen.

C is wrong: A pH of 4.0 to 5.0 matches the acidic vagina, which is harmful to sperm.

D is wrong: A pH of 8.5 to 9.5 is too alkaline and suggests an abnormal sample or infection.

7. Which sperm motility range is considered normal in a semen analysis according to the handout?

A. 40 to 81 percent

B. 5 to 15 percent

C. 20 to 30 percent

D. 90 to 100 percent

Answer: A. 40 to 81 percent

Normal sperm motility is 40 to 81 percent, meaning that many of the sperm are moving forward in a healthy way. Poor motility (asthenospermia) reduces the chance that sperm will reach the fallopian tube. Heat, smoking, varicocele, and infection can lower motility. Teach the man to avoid hot tubs and tight underwear before retesting.

B is wrong: Five to 15 percent motility is severely reduced (asthenospermia).

C is wrong: Twenty to 30 percent motility is below the normal range.

D is wrong: Ninety to 100 percent is not the expected normal range, since some immotile sperm are always present.

8. A semen report shows normal sperm morphology. Which range of normally shaped sperm is acceptable according to the handout?

A. 0 to 1 percent

B. 60 to 90 percent

C. 4 to 48 percent

D. 70 to 100 percent

Answer: C. 4 to 48 percent

The handout gives normal morphology as 4 to 48 percent normally shaped sperm. Even in fertile men many sperm have shape defects, so only a minority need to look normal. Strict criteria set the lower limit at about 4 percent. Teratospermia is a high rate of abnormal forms. Tip: morphology means shape.

A is wrong: Zero to 1 percent normal forms would be markedly abnormal (teratospermia).

B is wrong: Sixty to 90 percent is higher than the usual normal morphology range.

D is wrong: Seventy to 100 percent is unrealistic, since most sperm normally have some shape defects.

9. A 26-year-old woman who has been married for 8 months and has regular menses asks a nurse at a health center whether she is infertile. What is the best response?

A. Explain that infertility is diagnosed after one year of frequent unprotected intercourse, and teach about the fertile days

B. Start clomiphene to induce ovulation as early treatment

C. Tell the couple they are infertile and should consider in vitro fertilization

D. Refer her husband for an immediate semen analysis and tubal testing

Answer: A. Explain that infertility is diagnosed after one year of frequent unprotected intercourse, and teach about the fertile days

Infertility is not diagnosed until a couple has failed to conceive after ONE year of frequent, unprotected intercourse. At 8 months with regular cycles this woman is within the normal range, so reassurance and education come first. Teach ovulation signs, such as clear stretchy mucus and the mid-cycle days, and intercourse every 1 to 2 days around ovulation. Refer if no pregnancy occurs after a year.

B is wrong: Ovulation drugs are not indicated in a woman with regular menses and less than one year of trying.

C is wrong: Labeling the couple infertile at 8 months is inaccurate and causes needless anxiety.

D is wrong: Immediate invasive testing is premature because the couple has not yet reached the one-year mark.

10. A 24-year-old woman at a health center in Cebu City reports irregular menstruation, weight gain, and growth of facial hair. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

A. Hypothyroidism

B. Polycystic ovary syndrome

C. Premature ovarian failure

D. Turner syndrome

Answer: B. Polycystic ovary syndrome

Irregular periods plus weight gain plus facial hair (hirsutism) is the classic picture of PCOS, a leading cause of anovulatory infertility. High androgens and insulin resistance disturb ovulation. Caveat: the handout spells out the letters as Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome, but the accepted name is polycystic ovary syndrome. Treatment includes weight loss, metformin, and clomiphene.

A is wrong: Hypothyroidism may cause weight gain and irregular menses but does not typically cause facial hair.

C is wrong: Premature ovarian failure causes menopausal symptoms and low estrogen, not excess androgen signs.

D is wrong: Turner syndrome presents with short stature and primary amenorrhea, not hirsutism.

11. A 22-year-old primigravida at a barangay health center measures 143 cm in height. According to the HBMR prenatal screening tool, which complication is most associated with this finding?

A. Convulsive seizures from eclampsia

B. Gestational trophoblastic disease

C. Uterine atony after twin birth

D. Cephalopelvic disproportion that may need cesarean birth

Answer: D. Cephalopelvic disproportion that may need cesarean birth

A height of less than 145 cm is a risk factor on the HBMR because the pelvis may be small, leading to cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) and possible cesarean birth. The woman should be referred to a facility capable of surgery for delivery. Tip: short mother, small pelvis, big baby problem. A history of CPD carries the same implication.

A is wrong: Eclampsia is linked to hypertension in pregnancy, not to height.

B is wrong: Gestational trophoblastic disease relates to abnormal fertilization, not stature.

C is wrong: Uterine atony is linked to grand multiparity or overdistention, not to short height.

12. Which maternal ages are considered risk factors in the DOH Home-Based Mother's Record (HBMR) screening tool?

A. Younger than 18 years and older than 35 years

B. Younger than 20 years and older than 40 years

C. Younger than 16 years and older than 45 years

D. Younger than 15 years and older than 30 years

Answer: A. Younger than 18 years and older than 35 years

The HBMR flags women younger than 18 or older than 35 as high risk. Very young mothers have higher risk of preterm birth, hypertension, and CPD, while older mothers have more chronic disease, fetal anomalies, and cesarean birth. These women should give birth in a hospital or facility with emergency care. Memory aid: under 18, over 35.

B is wrong: Twenty and forty are not the HBMR age cutoffs.

C is wrong: Sixteen and forty-five are not the HBMR age cutoffs.

D is wrong: Fifteen and thirty do not match the HBMR age cutoffs.

13. A nurse at a lying-in clinic reviews records of a woman who is G6P5 and expects delivery. For which complication is she at greatest risk after birth?

A. Ectopic pregnancy

B. Hyperemesis gravidarum

C. Uterine atony with postpartum hemorrhage

D. Infertility

Answer: C. Uterine atony with postpartum hemorrhage

A woman with more than four pregnancies (grand multipara) has overstretched, fatigued uterine muscle that may fail to contract after birth, causing uterine atony and postpartum hemorrhage. Plan oxytocin, fundal checks, and a facility birth. Remember: more than four babies, more bleeding risk, watch the fundus.

A is wrong: Ectopic pregnancy relates to tubal damage and implantation, not parity.

B is wrong: Hyperemesis occurs mainly in the first trimester and is not due to high parity.

D is wrong: Infertility is not an expected outcome of repeated pregnancies.

14. Which item correctly identifies an interval that places a pregnant woman in the high-risk category on the HBMR?

A. Last baby was born 4 years ago

B. Last baby was born less than 2 years ago

C. Last baby was born 3 years ago

D. Last baby was born 5 years ago

Answer: B. Last baby was born less than 2 years ago

A birth interval of less than 2 years is a risk factor because the mother has not fully recovered her nutritional stores and uterine tissue, raising the risk of anemia, preterm birth, and low birth weight. Family planning counseling under RA 10354 should stress birth spacing of at least 2 to 3 years. Tip: less than 2 years means too soon.

A is wrong: A 4-year interval is acceptable spacing and not flagged as risk.

C is wrong: A 3-year interval is considered an adequate spacing and not a risk factor.

D is wrong: A 5-year interval is not a short-interval risk.

15. During prenatal screening, a nurse records the weight of four pregnant women. Which weight should be flagged as a risk factor on the HBMR?

A. Less than 50 kg or more than 90 kg

B. Less than 45 kg or more than 80 kg

C. Less than 55 kg or more than 100 kg

D. Less than 40 kg or more than 70 kg

Answer: B. Less than 45 kg or more than 80 kg

The handout lists under- or overweight as less than 45 kg or more than 80 kg. Underweight raises the risk of low birth weight and preterm birth, while overweight raises the risk of gestational diabetes, hypertension, and cesarean birth. Provide nutrition counseling and refer for risk management. Tip: 45 low, 80 high.

A is wrong: The 50 and 90 kg limits are not those listed in the HBMR.

C is wrong: The 55 and 100 kg limits are not those listed in the HBMR.

D is wrong: The 40 and 70 kg limits are not those listed in the HBMR.

16. A barangay health worker refers four pregnant women to the nurse. Which woman should be classified as high risk and referred first?

A. A 27-year-old woman G2P1, 155 cm, 58 kg, last birth 4 years ago

B. A 30-year-old woman G3P2 with normal vital signs and hemoglobin of 12 g/dL

C. A 25-year-old woman G1, 152 cm, 55 kg, with no complaints

D. A 33-year-old woman G3P2 with severe anemia

Answer: D. A 33-year-old woman G3P2 with severe anemia

The HBMR counts medical conditions such as TB, goiter, heart disease, diabetes, bronchial asthma, and severe anemia as risk factors. The woman with severe anemia is at risk for poor oxygen delivery, preterm birth, and hemorrhage, so she needs referral and facility delivery. The other women meet no HBMR criteria for age, height, weight, parity, or spacing.

A is wrong: She has no HBMR risk factors, so she can continue routine prenatal care.

B is wrong: Normal vital signs and normal hemoglobin place her at routine risk.

C is wrong: A healthy primigravida of normal height and weight has no listed risk factor.

17. A woman at a hospital in Davao City was told in her last labor that she had cephalopelvic disproportion. She is now pregnant again. Which birth plan does the nurse expect?

A. Forceps delivery at term

B. Cesarean birth

C. Vaginal birth with oxytocin induction

D. Home delivery with a skilled birth attendant

Answer: B. Cesarean birth

On the HBMR, a history of CPD (or a previous complicated birth) points to cesarean birth, because the fetal head cannot pass through the maternal pelvis. Women with this history must give birth in a hospital where surgery is available. Tip: CPD equals CS. Teach her to go to the facility at the first sign of labor.

A is wrong: Forceps is not appropriate for a pelvis that is too small for the fetus.

C is wrong: Oxytocin would worsen obstructed labor and risk uterine rupture.

D is wrong: Home delivery is unsafe when a past CPD predicts obstructed labor.

18. A woman at 35 weeks with pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) complains of severe epigastric pain. The nurse recognizes this symptom as a warning of which complication?

A. Impending eclampsia

B. Placenta previa

C. Hyperemesis gravidarum

D. Gastroesophageal reflux of pregnancy

Answer: A. Impending eclampsia

Epigastric pain in PIH signals liver swelling and capsule stretching, a sign of severe preeclampsia that may progress to eclampsia (convulsive seizures). Notify the physician at once, start seizure precautions, and prepare magnesium sulfate. Other warning signs are headache, visual changes, and hyperreflexia. Tip: epigastric pain in PIH means the seizure is near.

B is wrong: Placenta previa presents with painless bright red bleeding.

C is wrong: Hyperemesis is excessive vomiting in early pregnancy and not epigastric pain from PIH.

D is wrong: Reflux causes heartburn after meals and does not signal a hypertensive emergency.

19. A pregnant woman at a health center has fever, back pain, and tenderness at the costovertebral angle. What is the nursing implication of this finding?

A. It can be mistaken for labor pain, so a urinalysis and culture are needed

B. It confirms preeclampsia, so only blood pressure needs monitoring

C. It is normal pregnancy backache that needs no further assessment

D. It suggests ectopic pregnancy, so TVUS is the first step

Answer: A. It can be mistaken for labor pain, so a urinalysis and culture are needed

Urinary tract infection in pregnancy can ascend to the kidney, and costovertebral angle (CVA) pain can be mistaken for labor pain. A clean-catch urinalysis and culture should be done and antibiotics given as ordered. Untreated UTI can cause preterm labor. Tip: back pain plus fever equals think pyelonephritis, not just labor.

B is wrong: Flank pain with fever points to kidney infection, not to hypertension alone.

C is wrong: Fever with costovertebral tenderness is not normal and needs workup.

D is wrong: Ectopic pregnancy gives unilateral lower abdominal pain in the first trimester.

20. A nurse teaches women about risk factors and their related complications. Which pairing is correct according to the handout?

A. Urinary tract infection and placenta previa

B. Multiparity and breast cancer

C. Multiple sexual partners and sexually transmitted infection

D. Nulliparity and cervical cancer

Answer: C. Multiple sexual partners and sexually transmitted infection

The handout pairs multiple sexual partners with STI, nulliparity with breast cancer, and multiparity with cervical cancer. Caveat: cervical cancer is driven mainly by HPV, and number of partners and multiple births add risk. STIs in pregnancy can cause preterm labor and neonatal infection, so counsel on condom use and screening.

A is wrong: UTI is not related to placenta previa, it can mask labor pain.

B is wrong: The handout links multiparity to cervical cancer, not breast cancer.

D is wrong: The handout links nulliparity to breast cancer, not cervical cancer.

21. The nurse uses the APPLES mnemonic to teach common danger signs in pregnancy. What does the letter L stand for?

A. Loss of appetite

B. Lightheadedness with fainting

C. Labor contractions before 37 weeks only

D. Low backache or leaking of fluid from the vagina

Answer: D. Low backache or leaking of fluid from the vagina

APPLES stands for: Absence of fetal movement or abdominal pain, Persistent vomiting beyond the first trimester, Pelvic pressure, Low backache or leaking of fluid, Excessive weight gain, and Swelling of fingers or spotting. Low backache and leaking fluid may mean preterm labor or PROM. Teach every mother these signs and to go to the facility right away.

A is wrong: Appetite loss is not a listed APPLES danger sign.

B is wrong: Fainting is not part of the APPLES list in the handout.

C is wrong: Preterm contractions are important but are not what L stands for in this mnemonic.

22. A woman at 32 weeks tells the nurse at a barangay health center that she has not felt the baby move since morning and has abdominal pain. What is the priority action?

A. Reassure her that fetal movement slows in the third trimester

B. Schedule her for the next regular prenatal visit

C. Refer her immediately to a hospital for fetal assessment

D. Advise her to drink cold water and recount movements tomorrow

Answer: C. Refer her immediately to a hospital for fetal assessment

Absence of fetal movement plus abdominal pain is the A in APPLES and may indicate fetal hypoxia, abruptio placentae, or fetal death. The nurse must act immediately with transfer for NST, ultrasound, and monitoring. Fetal movement should be about 10 in 2 hours, so a sudden stop is never normal. Keep her calm, lying on her left side, and transport with a companion. Tip: no kick plus pain means go now.

A is wrong: Fetal movement does not normally stop, so reassurance is unsafe.

B is wrong: The next routine visit is too late for a possible emergency.

D is wrong: Waiting a full day delays detection of fetal compromise, such as abruptio placentae.

23. Two hours after birth in a lying-in clinic, a woman reports that her perineal pad is soaked within one hour. What should the nurse do first?

A. Remove the pad and encourage her to walk

B. Apply an ice pack to the perineum

C. Document the finding and recheck in 4 hours

D. Palpate the fundus and massage it if it is boggy

Answer: D. Palpate the fundus and massage it if it is boggy

A pad saturated within one hour and a boggy uterus point to uterine atony, the leading cause of postpartum hemorrhage. First massage the fundus until firm, then empty the bladder, give oxytocin per order, and monitor vital signs for shock (rising pulse and respirations, falling BP). Tip: boggy uterus means massage first.

A is wrong: Ambulation is not the first action and a bleeding woman may become faint.

B is wrong: Ice helps perineal pain and swelling but does not stop uterine bleeding.

C is wrong: Waiting 4 hours risks serious hemorrhage.

24. Three days after cesarean birth, a woman has calf tenderness, swelling, and redness of the left leg. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

A. Mastitis

B. Leg cramps from low calcium

C. Normal postpartum dependent edema

D. Deep vein thrombosis (thrombophlebitis)

Answer: D. Deep vein thrombosis (thrombophlebitis)

Calf tenderness, swelling, and redness is a postpartum danger sign of thrombophlebitis or DVT, because pregnancy raises clotting factors and surgery adds immobility. Do not massage the leg, because the clot may break off and cause pulmonary embolism. Elevate the leg, notify the physician, and expect anticoagulants. Tip: unilateral calf pain, think DVT.

A is wrong: Mastitis affects the breast and not the leg.

B is wrong: Cramps are not accompanied by redness and swelling in one calf.

C is wrong: Normal edema is bilateral and not tender or red.

25. Which statement about postpartum bleeding is accurate?

A. It is caused mainly by cervical lacerations and not by uterine atony

B. It is the most common complication after delivery, and twin birth increases the risk

C. It is no longer a risk once the placenta is delivered

D. It is a rare complication that occurs only after cesarean birth

Answer: B. It is the most common complication after delivery, and twin birth increases the risk

Postpartum bleeding is the most common complication after delivery, and an overdistended uterus from twins or large babies raises the risk of atony. Assess fundal firmness, lochia, pad count, and vital signs frequently in the first hours after birth. Keep oxytocin ready. Memory aid: twins, atony, hemorrhage.
