D. Chronic maternal infection destroys the glomeruli before conception

Answer: C. Abnormal placental blood vessel development reduces placental blood flow, causing hypoxia and endothelial dysfunction

Preeclampsia begins with abnormal development and function of placental vessels. Reduced placental flow leads to hypoxia and ischemia, endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction and increased vascular permeability. The result is hypertension and proteinuria, with possible multisystem damage. This is why delivery of the placenta is the definitive cure.

A is wrong: Insulin excess is not the cause, glucose problems relate to gestational diabetes.

B is wrong: The problem starts in the placenta, not in fetal cardiac function.

D is wrong: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy-specific placental disorder, not a preexisting infection of the glomeruli.

112. A 28-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks in a Cebu hospital has BP 148/94, 2+ urine protein and puffiness of the hands and face. Which classification fits this client?

A. Mild preeclampsia

B. Gestational hypertension

C. Severe preeclampsia

D. Eclampsia

Answer: A. Mild preeclampsia

Mild preeclampsia means BP above 140/90 mmHg with 1+ to 2+ proteinuria and edema such as excessive weight gain or puffy face and hands. Gestational hypertension has no proteinuria. Severe preeclampsia has BP of 160/110 or higher with 3+ to 4+ protein, and eclampsia adds seizures. Classify by comparing BP, protein and symptoms.

B is wrong: Gestational hypertension would have no proteinuria.

C is wrong: Severe preeclampsia requires BP of 160/110 or more and 3+ to 4+ protein.

D is wrong: Eclampsia requires a seizure, which she has not had.

113. Which finding distinguishes gestational hypertension from mild preeclampsia?

A. Absence of proteinuria

B. A blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg

C. Presence of seizures

D. Upper body edema

Answer: A. Absence of proteinuria

Both conditions show blood pressure above 140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks. Gestational hypertension has no proteinuria and no edema requirement, while mild preeclampsia adds 1+ to 2+ proteinuria. Management of gestational hypertension focuses on BP control and monitoring because it can progress to preeclampsia. Check urine protein at every prenatal visit.

B is wrong: A pressure of 160/110 mmHg indicates a severe-range reading, not the distinguishing feature.

C is wrong: Seizures define eclampsia.

D is wrong: Upper body edema occurs with preeclampsia, not gestational hypertension.

114. Which blood pressure reading classifies a pregnant woman's preeclampsia as severe?

A. 140/90 mmHg

B. 130/80 mmHg

C. 150/100 mmHg

D. 160/110 mmHg or higher

Answer: D. 160/110 mmHg or higher

Severe preeclampsia is marked by BP of 160/110 mmHg or higher, 3+ to 4+ proteinuria and symptoms such as severe headache, visual changes, epigastric pain and thrombocytopenia. Mild preeclampsia is above 140/90. Severe disease needs magnesium sulfate, BP control, and monitoring for organ dysfunction. Remember 160 over 110 as the severe line.

A is wrong: 140/90 mmHg is the mild threshold.

B is wrong: 130/80 mmHg is below the hypertensive threshold in pregnancy.

C is wrong: 150/100 mmHg is still in the mild range.

115. Which 24-hour urine protein result is associated with severe preeclampsia in the review?

A. More than 5 g

B. Less than 150 mg

C. About 300 mg

D. About 1 g

Answer: A. More than 5 g

The review lists 3+ to 4+ dipstick protein and a 24-hour urine protein of more than 5 g as severe proteinuria. Normal excretion is under 150 mg per day, and 300 mg or more is the usual threshold for preeclampsia. Note that current guidelines no longer depend on the 5 g figure to define severity, so BP and organ symptoms matter more.

B is wrong: Less than 150 mg a day is normal in pregnancy.

C is wrong: 300 mg is the threshold for diagnosing preeclampsia, not severe disease.

D is wrong: 1 g is moderate proteinuria and below the severe cut-off in the review.

116. A client with mild preeclampsia at a barangay health center now reports severe headache, blurred vision and epigastric pain. Which interpretation is correct?

A. These are expected discomforts of mild preeclampsia and need only rest

B. These signs show progression to severe preeclampsia and need urgent referral

C. These suggest gestational diabetes and need a glucose check

D. These indicate false labor and need reassurance

Answer: B. These signs show progression to severe preeclampsia and need urgent referral

Severe headache, visual problems, epigastric pain and thrombocytopenia are present in severe preeclampsia but not in mild disease. They signal cerebral irritation and liver involvement, so the risk of seizure and HELLP syndrome rises. The nurse should check BP, give ordered care and arrange immediate transfer. Do not treat these as minor complaints.

A is wrong: These symptoms are not part of mild disease.

C is wrong: Gestational diabetes does not cause these neurologic and hepatic symptoms.

D is wrong: False labor causes irregular contractions, not visual changes.

117. A woman with severe preeclampsia suddenly has a tonic-clonic seizure in the labor room. Which action is the priority?

A. Insert a padded tongue blade between her teeth

B. Restrain her limbs firmly

C. Give oral fluids once the seizure ends

D. Maintain a patent airway and prevent injury by turning her to the side

Answer: D. Maintain a patent airway and prevent injury by turning her to the side

During an eclamptic seizure the priority is airway and safety. Turn the client to the side to lower aspiration risk, raise padded side rails, suction and give oxygen, then give ordered magnesium sulfate and monitor the fetal heart rate. Never force objects into the mouth or restrain the limbs. Airway first, then drug, then delivery planning.

A is wrong: Forcing a blade in the mouth can injure the teeth and obstruct the airway.

B is wrong: Restraint can cause injury and does not stop the seizure.

C is wrong: Oral intake after a seizure risks aspiration while she is drowsy.

118. A client with mild preeclampsia is being managed at home. Which instruction is appropriate?

A. Follow a strict sodium-restricted diet

B. Take a diuretic every morning to reduce the swelling

C. Exercise vigorously to lower the blood pressure

D. Rest in a left side-lying position and keep a normal salt intake

Answer: D. Rest in a left side-lying position and keep a normal salt intake

Management of mild preeclampsia includes bed rest, BP control and a normal salt intake. Left side-lying improves venous return and uteroplacental perfusion. She should check BP, count fetal movements and report headache, visual changes or epigastric pain. Diuretics and strict salt restriction are not routine because they can reduce plasma volume.

A is wrong: Strict salt restriction is not advised, the handout lists normal salt intake.

B is wrong: Diuretics can deplete intravascular volume and harm placental flow.

C is wrong: Vigorous exercise can raise BP and is not recommended.

119. Which edema pattern is characteristic of preeclampsia?

A. Swelling of the ankles that goes away overnight

B. Swelling confined to one painful calf

C. Dependent swelling only after standing all day

D. Puffiness of the face and hands with sudden excessive weekly weight gain

Answer: D. Puffiness of the face and hands with sudden excessive weekly weight gain

Preeclampsia edema is upper body edema, with puffiness of the hands and face and excessive weight gain in a week. This reflects increased vascular permeability. Ankle swelling that resolves with rest is a normal pregnancy change, and a painful unilateral calf suggests deep vein thrombosis. Ask about rings feeling tight and morning facial puffiness.

A is wrong: Ankle swelling that resolves with rest is physiologic.

B is wrong: A single painful swollen calf suggests thrombophlebitis or DVT.

C is wrong: Dependent edema from standing is a normal change.

120. Which of the following is an oral antihypertensive commonly used to control blood pressure in pregnancy?

A. Enalapril

B. Methyldopa

C. Losartan

D. Spironolactone

Answer: B. Methyldopa

Methyldopa, labetalol and nifedipine are the common antihypertensives for pregnancy. ACE inhibitors such as enalapril and angiotensin receptor blockers such as losartan are contraindicated because they can cause fetal renal failure and malformations. Spironolactone is also avoided. Remember the safe trio: methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine.

A is wrong: Enalapril is an ACE inhibitor and is teratogenic.

C is wrong: Losartan is an ARB and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

D is wrong: Spironolactone has antiandrogenic effects on the fetus and is not used.

121. A woman with severe preeclampsia on a magnesium sulfate infusion has a respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute and absent patellar reflexes. What should the nurse do first?

A. Slow the infusion by half and recheck in one hour

B. Increase oxygen and continue the infusion

C. Stop the infusion and prepare calcium gluconate

D. Give a bolus of IV fluids

Answer: C. Stop the infusion and prepare calcium gluconate

Absent reflexes and a respiratory rate below 12 signal magnesium toxicity, which can lead to respiratory arrest. The nurse stops the infusion, notifies the physician and prepares calcium gluconate, the antidote, while giving oxygen and monitoring. Never continue the drug when reflexes are lost. Remember that magnesium sulfate toxicity is checked by reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output before every dose.

A is wrong: Merely slowing the drug keeps magnesium rising in a toxic client.

B is wrong: Oxygen alone does not remove the cause, the infusion must stop.

D is wrong: IV fluids do not reverse magnesium effects and risk fluid overload.

122. In the MAGIC reminder for a client on magnesium sulfate, what does the letter C stand for?

A. Continuous fetal monitoring

B. Creatinine clearance

C. Calcium gluconate kept at the bedside

D. Cesarean preparation

Answer: C. Calcium gluconate kept at the bedside

MAGIC reminds the nurse what to do for magnesium sulfate: Monitor reflexes, Assess respiratory rate (at least 12 per minute), Glasgow Coma Scale, Intake and output (urine at least 30 mL per hour), and Calcium gluconate as the antidote kept at the bedside. Check these before each dose and during the infusion. Keep the antidote drawn up and labeled so it can be given within seconds if breathing slows.

A is wrong: Fetal monitoring is important but is not the C in MAGIC.

B is wrong: Creatinine is not part of the mnemonic, though urine output is.

D is wrong: Cesarean prep is not part of the mnemonic.

123. Which finding is the earliest sign of magnesium sulfate toxicity?

A. Respiratory depression

B. Cardiac arrest

C. Loss of deep tendon reflexes

D. Oliguria

Answer: C. Loss of deep tendon reflexes

Therapeutic magnesium levels are about 4 to 7 mEq/L. Loss of patellar reflexes appears first, at around 8 to 10 mEq/L, followed by respiratory depression and then cardiac arrest at much higher levels. Checking reflexes lets the nurse stop the drug before the dangerous stages. Oliguria is a risk factor for toxicity rather than a sign.

A is wrong: Respiratory depression appears later than reflex loss.

B is wrong: Cardiac arrest is a late, life-threatening effect.

D is wrong: Low urine output raises toxicity risk but is not a toxic sign of the drug.

124. A client receiving magnesium sulfate in a district hospital has urine output of 20 mL per hour for two hours. Why is this finding important?

A. Low output proves the seizure risk has resolved

B. It shows the drug is acting as a diuretic

C. It means the infusion rate can be doubled

D. Magnesium is excreted by the kidneys, so low output increases the risk of toxicity

Answer: D. Magnesium is excreted by the kidneys, so low output increases the risk of toxicity

Magnesium is cleared through the kidneys, so urine output should be at least 30 mL per hour (about 100 mL per 4 hours). Lower output allows the drug to accumulate and cause toxicity. The nurse should hold the infusion, notify the physician and check reflexes and respirations. Accurate intake and output is the I in MAGIC.

A is wrong: Seizure risk is not judged by urine output.

B is wrong: Magnesium is not a diuretic.

C is wrong: Increasing the dose with poor excretion would cause toxicity.

125. A woman at 32 weeks with severe preeclampsia needs preterm delivery. What is the purpose of giving betamethasone?

A. To hasten fetal lung maturity

B. To prevent maternal seizures

C. To lower maternal blood pressure

D. To stop uterine contractions

Answer: A. To hasten fetal lung maturity

Corticosteroids such as betamethasone or dexamethasone are given when preterm delivery is necessary to speed fetal lung maturation by stimulating surfactant production. They reduce respiratory distress syndrome and intraventricular hemorrhage. A common course is two IM doses 24 hours apart before 34 weeks. Seizure prevention is the role of magnesium sulfate.

B is wrong: Magnesium sulfate, not steroids, prevents seizures.

C is wrong: Antihypertensives lower BP, steroids do not.

D is wrong: Tocolytics, not steroids, suppress contractions.

126. A nurse gives IV hydralazine to a woman with severe preeclampsia whose BP is 168/112. Which adverse effect should the nurse watch for?

A. Reflex tachycardia and headache

B. Bradycardia and hyperkalemia

C. Constipation and urinary retention

D. Hyperglycemia and weight loss

Answer: A. Reflex tachycardia and headache

Hydralazine is a direct arterial vasodilator used for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy. The drop in pressure triggers reflex tachycardia, and headache, flushing and palpitations are common. BP should fall gradually, usually to about 140 to 150 over 90 to 100, because a sudden drop reduces placental perfusion. Monitor maternal BP and the fetal heart rate.

B is wrong: Hydralazine does not cause bradycardia, it tends to cause tachycardia.

C is wrong: Constipation and urinary retention are anticholinergic effects not typical of hydralazine.

D is wrong: Hydralazine does not cause hyperglycemia.

127. What is the definitive treatment for severe preeclampsia and eclampsia?

A. Strict bed rest in a dark room

B. Delivery of the baby and placenta

C. Continuous oral antihypertensive therapy

D. Fluid restriction with diuretics

Answer: B. Delivery of the baby and placenta

Because the placenta is the root of the disease, only delivery of the fetus and placenta cures preeclampsia. Magnesium sulfate, antihypertensives and monitoring stabilize the mother until birth, and corticosteroids help the fetal lungs if preterm. Timing and route depend on maternal and fetal condition. Remember: stabilize first, then deliver.

A is wrong: Bed rest only lessens symptoms and does not cure the disease.

C is wrong: Antihypertensives control BP but do not remove the cause.

D is wrong: Diuretics and fluid restriction can worsen placental perfusion and do not cure it.

128. Which environment should the nurse prepare for a client with severe preeclampsia receiving magnesium sulfate?

A. A busy ward beside the nurses' station with bright lights

B. A quiet, dimly lit room with padded side rails, suction and oxygen ready

C. A room with a television on to keep her distracted

D. A room where visitors stay at the bedside round the clock

Answer: B. A quiet, dimly lit room with padded side rails, suction and oxygen ready

Seizure precautions reduce stimuli that can trigger convulsions. A quiet, dimly lit private room, padded side rails, bed in low position, suction and oxygen at the bedside, and restricted visitors protect the client. Check that calcium gluconate is available too. Think low light, low noise, low stimulation. Check that the call light, oxygen and suction work before the infusion starts.

A is wrong: Bright lights and noise are triggers for seizures.

C is wrong: Television adds light and noise stimulation.

D is wrong: Constant visitors increase stimulation and fatigue.

129. Which laboratory results should the nurse monitor to detect organ complications in a woman with severe preeclampsia?

A. Liver enzymes, serum creatinine and platelet count

B. Hemoglobin A1c and serum amylase

C. Thyroid hormones and serum calcium

D. Blood typing and rubella titer

Answer: A. Liver enzymes, serum creatinine and platelet count

Preeclampsia damages multiple organs. The liver function test (AST, ALT), kidney function test (creatinine, BUN, uric acid), platelet count and 24-hour urine protein show the extent of damage and warn of HELLP syndrome. These tests are repeated regularly to decide on delivery. Think liver, kidney, blood. A rising creatinine or falling platelet count often prompts a decision to deliver.

B is wrong: HbA1c and amylase do not reflect preeclampsia complications.

C is wrong: Thyroid hormones and calcium are not the key markers here.

D is wrong: Blood typing and rubella titer are prenatal screening tests, not complication monitors.

130. A client delivers vaginally after severe preeclampsia. For how long is magnesium sulfate usually continued after delivery?

A. Stopped as soon as the placenta is delivered

B. For 7 days

C. About 24 hours after delivery

D. Until the milk comes in

Answer: C. About 24 hours after delivery

Seizures can still occur after birth because the endothelial dysfunction does not resolve immediately. Magnesium sulfate is usually continued for about 24 hours postpartum, with continued monitoring of BP, reflexes, respirations and urine output. Postpartum eclampsia can occur up to several days after birth, so teach warning signs before discharge.

A is wrong: Stopping at placental delivery leaves her at risk of postpartum seizures.

B is wrong: Seven days is far longer than the usual postpartum course.

D is wrong: Lactogenesis is unrelated to the length of magnesium therapy.

131. Which is the antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity and how is it given?

A. Naloxone 0.4 mg given IV

B. Protamine sulfate given slowly IV

C. Vitamin K given IM

D. Calcium gluconate 1 g given slowly by IV push

Answer: D. Calcium gluconate 1 g given slowly by IV push

Calcium gluconate, usually 1 g (10 mL of a 10 percent solution) given slowly over about 3 minutes, antagonizes magnesium and reverses respiratory depression. It must be kept at the bedside for every client on magnesium sulfate. Give it slowly because rapid injection can cause arrhythmias. Pair the drug and its antidote in your memory.

A is wrong: Naloxone reverses opioids, not magnesium.

B is wrong: Protamine reverses heparin.

C is wrong: Vitamin K reverses warfarin and corrects vitamin K deficiency.

132. A multigravida in a barangay health center is fully dilated with the head crowning. The nearest hospital is 30 minutes away. What should the nurse do?

A. Place her in the ambulance and start for the hospital

B. Prepare for delivery on site and do not transport her

C. Instruct her to cross her legs and hold back pushing

D. Wait for the doctor before preparing anything

Answer: B. Prepare for delivery on site and do not transport her

When delivery is imminent, do not attempt to transport the client. Moving her risks birth in an unsafe vehicle. The nurse calls for help, prepares a clean delivery area, keeps the technique sterile, and follows Essential Intrapartum and Newborn Care steps. Crowning means birth within minutes. Call the doctor or midwife on duty, but never leave the woman alone while she is pushing.

A is wrong: Transport at this stage risks an unassisted birth in transit.

C is wrong: Holding back the baby can injure the infant and mother.

D is wrong: Waiting wastes time when the baby is about to be born.

133. A pregnant woman at 33 weeks is brought to the emergency room after a motorcycle crash and has abdominal tenderness. Which condition should the nurse assess for as the priority?

A. Placenta previa

B. Hydatidiform mole

C. Incompetent cervix

D. Abruptio placentae

Answer: D. Abruptio placentae

Blunt abdominal trauma such as a car or motorcycle accident can shear the placenta from the uterine wall, so the priority is to assess for abruptio placentae. Look for abdominal pain, a rigid board-like uterus, dark vaginal bleeding and fetal heart rate changes. Continuous fetal monitoring and a Kleihauer-Betke test are done, and Rh immune globulin is given to Rh-negative women.

A is wrong: Previa is not caused by trauma and gives painless bleeding.

B is wrong: A mole is a first trimester disorder.

C is wrong: Incompetent cervix causes painless dilation, not trauma-related tenderness.

134. What does the acronym HELLP stand for in a client with severe preeclampsia?

A. Hypertension, Edema, Low protein, Liver pain

B. Hemorrhage, Elevated leukocytes, Low potassium, Proteinuria

C. Hemolysis, Elevated liver enzymes, Low platelet count

D. Hypoglycemia, Elevated lipids, Low platelets, Polyuria

Answer: C. Hemolysis, Elevated liver enzymes, Low platelet count

HELLP syndrome is a life-threatening complication of preeclampsia with Hemolysis (red cells damaged in injured vessels), Elevated Liver enzymes and a Low Platelet count. It can occur without marked hypertension. Typical symptoms are right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting, malaise and headache. Treat it as an obstetric emergency.

A is wrong: This option invents terms that do not match the syndrome.

B is wrong: Leukocytes, potassium and proteinuria are not the defining items.

D is wrong: Lipids, glucose and polyuria are not part of HELLP.

135. A woman at 35 weeks has right upper quadrant pain, nausea and BP 164/112. Which laboratory findings would support HELLP syndrome?

A. Elevated platelets with low liver enzymes

B. Elevated AST and ALT with a low platelet count and signs of hemolysis

C. Low white cell count with high blood glucose

D. High hemoglobin with low bilirubin

Answer: B. Elevated AST and ALT with a low platelet count and signs of hemolysis

HELLP is confirmed by hemolysis (rising LDH and bilirubin, schistocytes), elevated liver enzymes (AST and ALT) and low platelets, often below 100,000 per mm3. These reflect red cell damage, liver injury and platelet consumption. Prompt delivery planning, magnesium sulfate and BP control follow. Remember the three letters tell you the three labs.

A is wrong: Platelets fall in HELLP, they do not rise.

C is wrong: White cells and glucose are not diagnostic of HELLP.

D is wrong: Hemolysis lowers hemoglobin and raises bilirubin.

136. Why does the platelet count fall in HELLP syndrome?

A. The bone marrow stops producing platelets because of iron loss

B. The spleen destroys platelets because of Rh incompatibility

C. Magnesium sulfate suppresses platelet production

D. Endothelial damage activates the coagulation cascade, which consumes platelets

Answer: D. Endothelial damage activates the coagulation cascade, which consumes platelets

In HELLP, high blood pressure injures the vascular endothelium and activates the coagulation cascade, so platelets are used up in clot formation. Red cells are damaged as they pass through the injured vessels (hemolysis), and clots deposited in hepatic vessels raise intrahepatic pressure and injure the liver. Low platelets raise the risk of bleeding.

A is wrong: Bone marrow suppression from iron deficiency is not the cause.

B is wrong: Rh incompatibility affects fetal red cells, not maternal platelets.

C is wrong: The syndrome develops before magnesium treatment and is not caused by it.

137. A woman at 34 weeks tells the nurse she has had epigastric pain and thinks it is gastritis. Her BP is 156/100. What is the best nurse action?

A. Give an antacid and reassess in the morning

B. Advise smaller meals and lying flat after eating

C. Report the pain at once and anticipate liver function and platelet tests

D. Teach her to avoid spicy foods

Answer: C. Report the pain at once and anticipate liver function and platelet tests

Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain in a hypertensive pregnant woman suggests liver involvement from severe preeclampsia or HELLP syndrome and must not be dismissed as indigestion. The nurse reports immediately and anticipates AST, ALT, LDH and platelet counts and closer monitoring. Delay can lead to liver rupture, seizure or abruption.

A is wrong: Antacids mask a serious complication and delay care.

B is wrong: Dietary changes do not address a hepatic cause.

D is wrong: Spicy food is not the cause here.

138. Which nursing precaution applies to a client with HELLP syndrome because of the risk of liver hematoma and rupture?

A. Encourage deep abdominal massage to relieve pain

B. Avoid vigorous abdominal palpation and report sudden severe upper abdominal pain

C. Apply a heating pad over the upper abdomen

D. Give all medications by intramuscular injection

Answer: B. Avoid vigorous abdominal palpation and report sudden severe upper abdominal pain

In HELLP, the liver is swollen and fragile and a subcapsular hematoma can rupture, so the abdomen should not be palpated or massaged vigorously. Sudden severe pain, shoulder pain or shock must be reported immediately. Low platelets also make IM injections and invasive procedures risky, so IV routes are preferred.

A is wrong: Deep massage could rupture a fragile liver.

C is wrong: Heat does not treat the cause and can mask worsening pain.

D is wrong: Low platelets increase the risk of intramuscular bleeding.

139. Why does gestational diabetes develop in some pregnant women?

A. Placental hormones such as human placental lactogen and cortisol oppose insulin action

B. The pancreas is destroyed by autoantibodies against beta cells

C. Fetal insulin crosses into the maternal blood and causes resistance

D. Increased maternal thyroid hormone lowers glucose use

Answer: A. Placental hormones such as human placental lactogen and cortisol oppose insulin action

During pregnancy the placenta produces human placental lactogen and cortisol, which interfere with insulin action and create insulin resistance. When the pancreas cannot raise insulin enough to meet the increased demand, glucose tolerance becomes impaired and gestational diabetes occurs. It usually appears in the second half of pregnancy and often resolves after delivery.

B is wrong: Autoimmune beta cell destruction describes type 1 diabetes.

C is wrong: Fetal insulin does not cross the placenta to the mother.

D is wrong: Thyroid hormone excess is not the cause of gestational diabetes.

140. Which pregnant client has the highest risk for gestational diabetes mellitus?

A. A 23-year-old primigravida of normal weight with no family history

B. A 35-year-old obese woman with a diabetic mother and a prior 4.5 kg baby

C. A 26-year-old who walks daily and has had two normal-weight babies

D. A 24-year-old with mild iron deficiency anemia

Answer: B. A 35-year-old obese woman with a diabetic mother and a prior 4.5 kg baby

Risk factors for GDM include maternal age above 30, obesity, family history of type 2 diabetes, GDM in a previous pregnancy, and a history of large-for-gestational-age infants, miscarriage, hydramnios or congenital anomalies. The first client has several of these. Anemia and young normal-weight status do not raise risk.

A is wrong: Young age and normal weight without family history are low-risk features.

C is wrong: Daily exercise and normal birth weights lower risk.

D is wrong: Iron deficiency anemia is not a risk factor for GDM.

141. Which test is considered the gold standard for diagnosing gestational diabetes?

A. Oral glucose tolerance test

B. Random capillary blood glucose

C. Urine dipstick for glucose

D. Glycosylated hemoglobin alone

Answer: A. Oral glucose tolerance test

The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is the gold standard to diagnose GDM. It measures how the body handles a glucose load, usually at 24 to 28 weeks, or earlier in high-risk women. Random glucose, urine glucose and HbA1c alone are insufficiently sensitive in pregnancy because glycosuria is common and HbA1c is altered by increased red cell turnover.

B is wrong: Random glucose does not test the response to a glucose load.

C is wrong: Glycosuria is common in normal pregnancy so urine dipstick is unreliable.

D is wrong: HbA1c alone is not used to diagnose GDM.

142. When is the 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test done in a pregnant woman?

A. Only after the woman delivers

B. At the first prenatal visit for all women

C. Only when the woman has glycosuria

D. When the 1-hour glucose screening result is abnormal

Answer: D. When the 1-hour glucose screening result is abnormal

Screening starts with the 1-hour nonfasting test using 50 g glucose. If this is abnormal, the 3-hour OGTT with a fasting glucose load is done, with blood drawn fasting, then at 1, 2 and 3 hours. Two or more abnormal values confirm GDM. The woman must fast overnight before the 3-hour test. Remember: abnormal screen, then 3-hour test, and diagnosis needs two or more high values.

A is wrong: Diagnosis in pregnancy is made antenatally, not after delivery.

B is wrong: Not all women need the 3-hour test, only those with an abnormal screen.

C is wrong: Glycosuria alone is not the criterion for the test.

143. A woman's 3-hour OGTT shows fasting 98 mg/dL, 1 hour 170 mg/dL, 2 hour 160 mg/dL and 3 hour 130 mg/dL. Using the cut-offs fasting 95, 1 hour 180, 2 hour 155 and 3 hour 140, how does the nurse interpret this?

A. Two values are above the cut-off, so gestational diabetes is diagnosed

B. Only one value is above the cut-off, so the result is normal

C. All four values are above the cut-off, so type 1 diabetes is diagnosed

D. No value is above the cut-off, so no follow-up is needed

Answer: A. Two values are above the cut-off, so gestational diabetes is diagnosed

The fasting value of 98 is above 95 and the 2-hour value of 160 is above 155, which makes two abnormal results. The 1-hour value of 170 is below 180 and the 3-hour value of 130 is below 140. Two or more abnormal values diagnose gestational diabetes. Count the values carefully against each limit. Exam tip: write the four limits down first, then mark each result as normal or abnormal.

B is wrong: Two, not one, values exceed their limits.

C is wrong: Only two values exceed their limits and OGTT cannot classify type 1 diabetes.

D is wrong: Two values are abnormal, so follow-up and treatment are needed.

144. What is the fasting blood glucose cut-off on the 3-hour OGTT above which the value is considered abnormal?

A. 95 mg/dL

B. 75 mg/dL

C. 110 mg/dL

D. 126 mg/dL

Answer: A. 95 mg/dL

The review lists the abnormal limits for the 3-hour OGTT as fasting above 95, 1 hour above 180, 2 hour above 155 and 3 hour above 140 mg/dL. Two or more abnormal values confirm GDM. A mnemonic is 95, 180, 155, 140. A fasting value of 126 or more is in the overt diabetes range in nonpregnant adults. A common mistake is mixing it up with the 140 mg/dL limit, which belongs to the 3-hour value.

B is wrong: 75 mg/dL is within normal limits and below the cut-off.

C is wrong: 110 mg/dL is above the pregnancy cut-off but is not the threshold used.

D is wrong: 126 mg/dL is the overt diabetes threshold, not the OGTT pregnancy limit.

145. A woman with gestational diabetes in a Davao hospital does not reach glucose targets with diet and exercise. Which drug does the nurse expect to be ordered?

A. Prednisone

B. Hydrochlorothiazide

C. Insulin

D. Enalapril

Answer: C. Insulin

When diet and exercise fail to control GDM, medications are added. Insulin is the standard because it does not cross the placenta, and metformin is another option listed in the review. Steroids and thiazides raise blood glucose, and ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy. Dose is titrated according to glucose monitoring.

A is wrong: Prednisone raises blood glucose and worsens hyperglycemia.

B is wrong: Thiazide diuretics can impair glucose tolerance.

D is wrong: Enalapril is an ACE inhibitor, harmful to the fetus, and not an antidiabetic.

146. During postpartum teaching for a woman who had gestational diabetes, which statement shows she understands her long-term risk?

A. I need my blood sugar rechecked after delivery because I may develop type 2 diabetes later

B. My diabetes will surely disappear for good once the baby is born

C. I will need insulin for life starting after delivery

D. I cannot breastfeed because of my condition

Answer: A. I need my blood sugar rechecked after delivery because I may develop type 2 diabetes later

GDM usually resolves after birth, but it greatly raises the risk of type 2 diabetes later in life. A glucose test (often a 75 g OGTT) is advised about 6 to 12 weeks postpartum, and then regular screening, weight control, healthy diet and exercise. Breastfeeding is encouraged and may help lower the risk. Her baby also needs early feeding and glucose checks, but her own risk continues for years.

B is wrong: Diabetes may recur or progress, so follow-up is needed.

C is wrong: Most women do not need lifelong insulin after GDM.

D is wrong: Breastfeeding is safe and recommended.

147. A newborn of a mother with gestational diabetes weighs 4.3 kg and is jittery at one hour of life. What should the nurse do first?

A. Check the blood glucose level

B. Wrap the baby tightly and offer plain water

C. Give an IV bolus of sodium bicarbonate

D. Start phototherapy

Answer: A. Check the blood glucose level

Infants of mothers with GDM are often macrosomic and at risk for birth trauma and hypoglycemia after birth. Jitteriness is a classic sign of hypoglycemia, so the nurse checks blood glucose first, then feeds early with breast milk or gives IV dextrose according to the level. Hypoglycemia is usually below 40 to 45 mg/dL in the first hours.

B is wrong: Water lacks calories and does not correct hypoglycemia.

C is wrong: Bicarbonate treats metabolic acidosis, not suspected hypoglycemia.

D is wrong: Jaundice is not the first concern at one hour of life.

148. Why are infants of mothers with poorly controlled gestational diabetes prone to hypoglycemia soon after birth?

A. Their liver cannot store glycogen because of prematurity

B. Their pancreas produces high insulin in response to maternal glucose, and the glucose supply stops at cord clamping

C. Their kidneys excrete glucose too quickly

D. Maternal glucagon keeps entering their blood after birth

Answer: B. Their pancreas produces high insulin in response to maternal glucose, and the glucose supply stops at cord clamping

Maternal hyperglycemia crosses the placenta and stimulates fetal beta cells to make extra insulin (hyperinsulinism). When the cord is clamped the glucose supply ends, but the high insulin level continues, causing hypoglycemia. This also explains macrosomia. Early feeding and glucose checks are the main nursing measures.

A is wrong: Prematurity is not the cause in most of these term macrosomic infants.

C is wrong: Renal glucose loss is not the mechanism.

D is wrong: Maternal glucagon does not continue to cross after birth.

149. Which teaching about home glucose monitoring is correct for a woman with gestational diabetes?

A. Check fasting and after-meal levels and aim for a fasting value below 95 mg/dL

B. Check once a week and aim for a fasting value above 120 mg/dL

C. Check only when symptoms appear and aim for above 180 mg/dL

D. Skip monitoring if the urine test is negative

Answer: A. Check fasting and after-meal levels and aim for a fasting value below 95 mg/dL

Women with GDM check blood glucose several times a day, typically fasting and 1 or 2 hours after meals, with a target fasting value below 95 mg/dL, consistent with the OGTT limits. Records help adjust diet and medication. Urine tests cannot guide therapy because they do not reflect blood glucose reliably. Poor control raises the risk of macrosomia and birth trauma.

B is wrong: Weekly checks and high targets would not keep glucose controlled.

C is wrong: Waiting for symptoms allows prolonged hyperglycemia.

D is wrong: A negative urine test does not exclude hyperglycemia.

150. A woman at 9 weeks with hyperemesis gravidarum is vomiting several times a day, has dry mucous membranes and ketonuria. Which is the priority nursing concern?

A. Providing a high-fat, large-volume diet

B. Encouraging strenuous exercise to relieve nausea

C. Maintaining hydration and electrolyte balance

D. Restricting all fluids to reduce vomiting

Answer: C. Maintaining hydration and electrolyte balance

In hyperemesis gravidarum, persistent vomiting causes dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, ketosis and weight loss, so the priority is fluid and electrolyte replacement, often with IV fluids, then antiemetics and small frequent dry meals. Monitor intake and output, weight, urine ketones and electrolytes. Hydration comes before diet teaching.

A is wrong: Large fatty meals worsen nausea and vomiting.

B is wrong: Exercise does not correct dehydration.

D is wrong: Fluid restriction worsens dehydration and ketosis.

151. Which immune cells does the human immunodeficiency virus bind to and destroy?

A. CD4+ T lymphocytes

B. CD8+ T lymphocytes

C. Neutrophils

D. Red blood cells

Answer: A. CD4+ T lymphocytes

HIV enters the body by binding to CD4 receptors and replicates inside CD4+ T helper cells. Progressive loss of these cells weakens immunity and increases susceptibility to opportunistic infections and cancers. This is why the CD4 count is used to follow disease progression and to define AIDS. Think CD4 equals command cells of the immune system.

B is wrong: CD8 cells are not the main target of HIV.

C is wrong: Neutrophils are not the primary target and do not have the CD4 receptor.

D is wrong: Red cells lack CD4 receptors and are not infected.

152. What is the normal CD4 count and the level that defines AIDS?

A. Normal 200 to 500 cells/mm3, AIDS below 50 cells/mm3

B. Normal 1000 to 1500 cells/mm3, AIDS below 500 cells/mm3

C. Normal 100 to 300 cells/mm3, AIDS below 20 cells/mm3

D. Normal 500 to 1000 cells/mm3, AIDS below 200 cells/mm3

Answer: D. Normal 500 to 1000 cells/mm3, AIDS below 200 cells/mm3

A healthy adult has a CD4 count of about 500 to 1000 cells/mm3. AIDS is diagnosed when the count falls below 200 cells/mm3, or when an AIDS-defining illness occurs. Low CD4 means high risk for opportunistic infections such as pneumocystis pneumonia and TB. Remember 500 to 1000 normal, below 200 is AIDS. Exam tip: the CD4 count tracks how much immune damage has occurred, while viral load tracks how much virus is present.

A is wrong: These ranges do not match the accepted normal range and AIDS threshold.

B is wrong: These ranges overstate the normal range and AIDS threshold.

C is wrong: These figures are far below normal and do not define AIDS.

153. A pregnant client with HIV in a Quezon City clinic has a CD4 count of 180 cells/mm3 and oral thrush. How does the nurse classify her condition?

A. Acute HIV infection, because the count is low

B. AIDS, because the count is below 200 cells/mm3

C. Asymptomatic chronic infection, because she is pregnant

D. Normal immune status, because thrush is common in pregnancy

Answer: B. AIDS, because the count is below 200 cells/mm3

A CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3 defines AIDS, the final and most advanced stage of untreated HIV. Oral candidiasis is a sign of immune suppression. Acute infection is the early flu-like stage, and chronic infection is initially asymptomatic. She needs antiretroviral therapy and prophylaxis against opportunistic infections, and care to prevent transmission to the baby.

A is wrong: Acute infection is the first few weeks after exposure, not a low CD4 stage.

C is wrong: She has symptoms and a CD4 level below 200, so she is not asymptomatic.

D is wrong: Thrush with this CD4 level shows immune failure, not normal immunity.

154. A woman exposed to HIV two weeks ago develops fever, sore throat, rash and swollen lymph nodes. Which stage does this suggest?

A. Chronic asymptomatic infection

B. AIDS

C. Acute HIV infection, a period of high infectiousness

D. The window period with no viral replication

Answer: C. Acute HIV infection, a period of high infectiousness

Acute HIV infection occurs in the first few weeks after exposure with flu-like symptoms such as fever, fatigue, sore throat, muscle and joint aches, swollen nodes, headache and rash. Viral load is very high, so she is highly infectious for about 4 to 6 weeks. Antibody tests may still be negative during this time, so testing should be repeated.

A is wrong: The chronic stage is asymptomatic or mild and lasts years.

B is wrong: AIDS is the final stage with CD4 below 200.

D is wrong: The virus replicates rapidly during the window period, it is simply not detected by the test.

155. Which statement describes chronic HIV infection?

A. A brief flu-like illness in the first few weeks

B. A long stage that can last for years with mild or no symptoms

C. The final stage with opportunistic infections

D. A stage with no virus in the body

Answer: B. A long stage that can last for years with mild or no symptoms

After acute infection comes the chronic (asymptomatic) stage, which may last for years. Symptoms are mild or non-specific, and some people have swollen lymph nodes, but the virus keeps replicating and damaging CD4 cells. Without treatment the person progresses to symptomatic disease and AIDS. Treatment can keep the person in this stage for life.

A is wrong: The brief flu-like illness describes acute infection.

C is wrong: Opportunistic infections characterize AIDS.

D is wrong: The virus persists in the body during chronic infection.

156. A pregnant client known to have HIV reports weight loss, night sweats and white patches in her mouth. What do these findings indicate?

A. Normal discomforts of the second trimester

B. Acute viral syndrome of the first weeks

C. Symptomatic HIV infection with oral thrush

D. Iron deficiency anemia

Answer: C. Symptomatic HIV infection with oral thrush

Symptomatic HIV infection brings weight loss, night sweats, oral candidiasis (thrush), respiratory infections, neurologic symptoms and herpes zoster as the immune system weakens. White patches that scrape off in the mouth suggest candidiasis. The finding calls for CD4 count and viral load checks and review of her treatment adherence.

A is wrong: Weight loss and night sweats are not normal pregnancy changes.

B is wrong: The acute syndrome occurs soon after exposure and includes fever and rash.

D is wrong: Anemia does not explain thrush and night sweats.

157. Which condition is considered an AIDS-defining illness?

A. Basal cell carcinoma

B. Uterine fibroids

C. Hypothyroidism

D. Kaposi's sarcoma

Answer: D. Kaposi's sarcoma

AIDS-defining conditions include CD4 below 200 cells/mm3, opportunistic infections such as TB, cytomegalovirus infection and pneumocystis pneumonia, Kaposi's sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and invasive cervical cancer. They appear because of profound immune deficiency. Kaposi's sarcoma presents as purple skin or mucosal lesions.

A is wrong: Basal cell carcinoma is not linked to AIDS definition.

B is wrong: Fibroids are benign tumors unrelated to HIV status.

C is wrong: Hypothyroidism is an endocrine disorder not tied to AIDS.

158. Which test is used as the initial screening in the two-step HIV testing process described in the review?

A. Western blot

B. CD4 count

C. Viral culture

D. Fourth generation ELISA that detects HIV antibody and antigen

Answer: D. Fourth generation ELISA that detects HIV antibody and antigen

The review describes a two-step process. Step one is a fourth generation ELISA (enzyme immunoassay), which detects both HIV antibodies and the p24 antigen for initial screening. Step two is a confirmatory test on reactive samples. CD4 count measures immune status, not infection, and culture is not used routinely. Screening is reactive first, then confirmed.

A is wrong: Western blot is the second, confirmatory step.

B is wrong: CD4 count monitors immune damage and is not a diagnostic test.

C is wrong: Viral culture is not routine for screening.

159. What is the purpose of the Western blot in HIV testing as described in the review?

A. To count CD4 cells

B. To screen all pregnant women at the first visit

C. To measure the viral load

D. To confirm a reactive screening result and eliminate false positives

Answer: D. To confirm a reactive screening result and eliminate false positives

The Western blot detects specific HIV antibodies and is used to validate a reactive result from the initial screening test, eliminating false positives and confirming the diagnosis. Note that current practice often uses a second, different immunoassay or nucleic acid testing for confirmation instead, and national confirmatory laboratories follow DOH algorithms, but the exam answer follows the review.

A is wrong: CD4 count is done by flow cytometry.

B is wrong: Screening uses ELISA or rapid tests, not Western blot.

C is wrong: Viral load is measured by nucleic acid testing.

160. Which marker detected by fourth generation HIV tests allows earlier detection than antibody-only tests?

A. CD4 receptor

B. Interleukin-6

C. p24 antigen

D. C-reactive protein

Answer: C. p24 antigen

Fourth generation enzyme immunoassays detect both HIV antibodies and the p24 antigen. The p24 antigen appears in blood before antibodies develop, which shortens the window period compared with third generation tests that detect antibodies only. This is why fourth generation tests are preferred for early detection. The p24 antigen is a core viral protein that peaks in the early weeks of infection.

A is wrong: The CD4 receptor is the cell receptor the virus uses and is not a test marker.

B is wrong: Interleukin-6 is an inflammatory cytokine not used for HIV diagnosis.

D is wrong: C-reactive protein is a nonspecific marker of inflammation.

161. A client asks which HIV test can detect infection sooner after a possible exposure. Based on the review, what is the best answer?

A. Third generation test, window period about 16 to 18 days

B. Fourth generation test, window period about 16 to 18 days

C. Fourth generation test, window period about 60 days

D. Third generation test, window period about 6 months

Answer: B. Fourth generation test, window period about 16 to 18 days

The review gives a window period of 20 to 22 days for the third generation test (antibody only) and 16 to 18 days for the fourth generation test (antibody plus p24 antigen). The earlier appearance of p24 makes the fourth generation test detect HIV sooner. Window periods in other references vary, and a negative test inside the window period should be repeated.

A is wrong: The 16 to 18 day window belongs to the fourth generation test, not the third.

C is wrong: A 60 day window is longer than that given for the fourth generation test.

D is wrong: A 6 month window is far longer than either figure in the review.

162. Through which routes can HIV pass from a mother to her child?

A. Pregnancy, childbirth and kissing

B. Childbirth, bathing and sharing utensils

C. Pregnancy, childbirth and breastfeeding

D. Breastfeeding, handshakes and mosquito bites

Answer: C. Pregnancy, childbirth and breastfeeding

Vertical (mother-to-child) transmission of HIV can happen during pregnancy across the placenta, during childbirth through exposure to blood and fluids, and through breastfeeding. Antiretroviral therapy, safe delivery and appropriate infant feeding and prophylaxis can reduce transmission to very low levels. HIV is not spread by casual contact.

A is wrong: HIV is not spread by kissing.

B is wrong: Bathing and utensils do not spread HIV.

D is wrong: HIV is not transmitted by handshakes or mosquito bites.

163. A mother with HIV who is taking antiretroviral therapy asks how to feed her baby. According to the WHO guidance in the review, what is correct?

A. Formula feeding only for the first year

B. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, then complementary feeding until 12 months

C. Breastfeeding for 6 weeks and then weaning

D. Mixed breast and formula feeding from birth

Answer: B. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, then complementary feeding until 12 months

The review cites WHO guidance that mothers with HIV on ART should exclusively breastfeed for the first 6 months and continue with complementary foods until 12 months. Mixed feeding is discouraged because it raises transmission risk. Note that WHO later extended breastfeeding to 24 months or beyond when on ART, and Philippine practice emphasizes counseling and adherence.

A is wrong: Formula only was the older advice and the review supports breastfeeding on ART.

C is wrong: A 6-week course is not the recommended duration.

D is wrong: Mixed feeding damages the infant gut and raises transmission risk.

164. A pregnant woman newly diagnosed with HIV is at 20 weeks gestation. Based on the review, which antiretroviral is preferred for her regimen?

A. Zidovudine alone as monotherapy

B. Acyclovir

C. Dolutegravir

D. Cotrimoxazole alone

Answer: C. Dolutegravir

The review states that dolutegravir is not recommended during the first trimester but is the preferred treatment after the first trimester, so at 20 weeks it is appropriate in a combination regimen. Note that current WHO guidance now considers dolutegravir safe in all trimesters. Monotherapy is never adequate for HIV.

A is wrong: Zidovudine alone is monotherapy and would cause resistance.

B is wrong: Acyclovir treats herpes, not HIV.

D is wrong: Cotrimoxazole prevents infections but does not suppress HIV.

165. What should the nurse tell the mother about vaccines for her HIV-exposed infant?

A. Follow the routine primary immunization schedule

B. Delay all vaccines until the child is 5 years old

C. Give only live vaccines

D. Skip all vaccines because of the exposure

Answer: A. Follow the routine primary immunization schedule

The review states that the routine primary immunization schedule should be followed for HIV-exposed infants born to women with HIV. Vaccines protect these infants from infections they are more vulnerable to. Infants confirmed with symptomatic HIV need individualized advice on live vaccines, but exposure alone does not change the schedule.

B is wrong: Delaying vaccines leaves the infant unprotected.

C is wrong: Live vaccines are not the only type and should not be singled out.

D is wrong: Skipping vaccines increases the risk of preventable disease.

166. What is the main purpose of giving antiretroviral therapy to a pregnant woman with HIV?

A. To suppress the viral load and reduce mother-to-child transmission

B. To cure the infection before delivery

C. To raise the CD4 count above 2000 cells/mm3

D. To prevent only fungal infections

Answer: A. To suppress the viral load and reduce mother-to-child transmission

ART suppresses viral replication, lowering the viral load to undetectable levels, which protects maternal health and sharply reduces transmission to the infant during pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding. It does not cure HIV, and adherence is essential. The baby also receives prophylaxis and testing according to national protocol.

B is wrong: ART controls but does not cure HIV.

C is wrong: Normal CD4 counts are far below 2000 and restoring numbers is not the main aim.

D is wrong: ART acts against HIV itself, not only against fungi.

167. Which are possible outcomes of untreated syphilis in a pregnant woman?

A. Neural tube defect and macrosomia only

B. Limb absence and chromosomal trisomy

C. Stillbirth and a baby with skin rashes, deafness or blindness

D. Isolated cleft lip with ear tags

Answer: C. Stillbirth and a baby with skin rashes, deafness or blindness

Syphilis-causing bacteria (Treponema pallidum) cross the placenta and infect the fetus. Untreated syphilis can lead to stillbirth, and congenital syphilis with meningitis, skin rashes, blindness and deafness. Screening is done at the first prenatal visit and repeated if at risk, so that treatment can be given early. Think rash, deaf, blind, stillbirth.

A is wrong: Neural tube defect is linked to folate deficiency and macrosomia to diabetes.

B is wrong: Limb absence and trisomy are not caused by syphilis.

D is wrong: Isolated cleft lip with ear tags is unrelated to syphilis.

168. A pregnant woman in a Cebu clinic tests reactive on RPR and is confirmed by a treponemal test. Which treatment does the nurse expect?

A. Oral doxycycline

B. Oral tetracycline

C. Benzathine penicillin G injection

D. Acyclovir

Answer: C. Benzathine penicillin G injection

Penicillin G is the only recommended treatment for syphilis in pregnancy because it treats both mother and fetus. Benzathine penicillin G is given IM, and women allergic to penicillin should be desensitized. Doxycycline and tetracycline are contraindicated in pregnancy because they affect fetal teeth and bones. Partner treatment and follow-up titers are also needed.

A is wrong: Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy and is not the standard treatment.

B is wrong: Tetracycline stains fetal teeth and affects bone growth.

D is wrong: Acyclovir is an antiviral and does not treat bacteria.

169. What is the risk to a fetus when the mother contracts varicella (chickenpox) early in pregnancy?

A. Fetal macrosomia and shoulder dystocia

B. Rh isoimmunization with hemolytic disease

C. Neural tube defects from folate deficiency

D. Congenital varicella syndrome with skin scarring and limb or eye defects

Answer: D. Congenital varicella syndrome with skin scarring and limb or eye defects

Chickenpox in a pregnant woman can cause congenital varicella syndrome in the baby, which results in congenital defects such as skin scarring, limb hypoplasia, eye problems and neurologic damage. Risk is highest with infection in the first half of pregnancy. Susceptible exposed women may receive varicella immune globulin.

A is wrong: Macrosomia is associated with maternal diabetes.

B is wrong: Rh isoimmunization is unrelated to varicella.

C is wrong: Neural tube defects result from folate deficiency.

170. A woman plans to conceive in 6 months and has no immunity to varicella. What should the nurse advise?

A. Get the vaccine as soon as she conceives

B. Get the varicella vaccine at least one month before becoming pregnant

C. Get the vaccine in the third trimester

D. Avoid vaccination because it is never safe

Answer: B. Get the varicella vaccine at least one month before becoming pregnant

Varicella vaccination can be done at least a month before planning to get pregnant. It is a live vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy, so it is given before conception or after delivery. Advice includes avoiding pregnancy for the recommended interval after the dose. Prevention is better than treating infection in pregnancy.

A is wrong: A live vaccine should not be given once she is pregnant.

C is wrong: The vaccine is not given in any trimester of pregnancy.

D is wrong: The vaccine is safe and advisable before pregnancy.

171. Rubella infection is most damaging to the fetus when it occurs in which period?

A. The third trimester

B. The first trimester

C. Only during labor

D. The postpartum period

Answer: B. The first trimester

Rubella (German measles) can be passed to the baby during the first trimester, when organs are forming, causing congenital rubella syndrome: cataract, deafness, heart defects such as patent ductus arteriosus and microcephaly. Prevention is MMR vaccination before pregnancy. The vaccine is live and is not given during pregnancy.

A is wrong: Infection in the third trimester carries a much lower risk of malformations.

C is wrong: Labor is not the time of greatest risk for congenital malformations.

D is wrong: Postpartum infection of the mother does not cause congenital defects.

172. A postpartum client in a Quezon City hospital is found to be non-immune to rubella. What is the appropriate nursing action?

A. Give MMR vaccine before discharge and advise her to avoid pregnancy for one month

B. Withhold the vaccine because she is breastfeeding

C. Give rubella immune globulin and delay the vaccine for one year

D. Do nothing because rubella only affects infants

Answer: A. Give MMR vaccine before discharge and advise her to avoid pregnancy for one month

A non-immune woman should be vaccinated after delivery, before discharge, to protect future pregnancies. The vaccine is live, so she must avoid pregnancy for about one month (28 days). Breastfeeding is not a contraindication. Rubella is dangerous mainly to the fetus in the first trimester. Postpartum vaccination is a missed-opportunity prevention measure, since future pregnancies would be at risk.

B is wrong: Breastfeeding does not prevent MMR vaccination.

C is wrong: A year delay leaves her unprotected for future pregnancies.

D is wrong: Rubella affects pregnant women's fetuses and she needs protection.

173. Which statement about cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is accurate?

A. It is a bacterial infection cured by penicillin

B. It is a fungal infection spread by cat feces

C. It belongs to the herpes virus group and has no cure

D. It is a parasite spread by raw meat

Answer: C. It belongs to the herpes virus group and has no cure

CMV is a member of the herpes virus group. It has no cure, it is usually self-limiting in non-pregnant clients but may cause serious complications in pregnant clients and their fetuses. Prevention includes handwashing and avoiding contact with the saliva and urine of infected people, especially small children. Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

A is wrong: CMV is a virus, so penicillin is ineffective.

B is wrong: Cat feces spread toxoplasmosis, which is caused by a parasite.

D is wrong: Raw meat is linked to toxoplasmosis, not CMV.

174. A newborn is diagnosed with congenital CMV. Which findings may the nurse observe?

A. Macrosomia, polycythemia and hypoglycemia

B. Cleft palate and polydactyly only

C. Lanugo and vernix caseosa only

D. Jaundice, hearing loss, seizures and small birth size

Answer: D. Jaundice, hearing loss, seizures and small birth size

Babies with congenital CMV may have jaundice, hearing and vision loss, seizures, muscle weakness, mental disabilities, lung problems and small birth size. Microcephaly is common too. Infants need audiology and eye follow-up, and the nurse should use standard precautions when handling secretions. Remember that CMV loves the brain, eyes and ears.

A is wrong: Macrosomia and hypoglycemia are seen in infants of diabetic mothers.

B is wrong: Cleft palate and extra digits are structural defects not typical of CMV.

C is wrong: Lanugo and vernix are normal newborn findings.

175. A pregnant woman has painful blisters and sores on the vulva. The nurse recognizes these as characteristic of which infection?

A. Primary syphilis

B. Condyloma acuminata

C. Candidiasis

D. Genital herpes

Answer: D. Genital herpes

Genital herpes, caused mainly by HSV-2 (HSV-1 can also be passed to the genitals), produces blisters that break down into painful sores. A primary syphilis chancre is a painless ulcer. Condyloma are painless warts, and candidiasis gives curdy discharge and itching. Pain is the key to herpes lesions. Exam tip: painful blisters mean herpes, a painless ulcer means syphilis.

A is wrong: A syphilitic chancre is typically painless.

B is wrong: Genital warts are painless growths, not blisters.

C is wrong: Candidiasis causes itching and thick white discharge.

176. In neonatal herpes, when does transmission from mother to baby most commonly occur?

A. In utero across the placenta in most cases

B. During delivery through a genital outbreak

C. Only through breast milk

D. During the second trimester ultrasound

Answer: B. During delivery through a genital outbreak

The review states that the genital outbreak is the most common way herpes is transmitted to the baby, while in utero transmission is rare and exposure may also happen in the neonatal period. For this reason cesarean birth is indicated when active genital lesions are present at labor. Neonatal herpes can be severe, affecting the skin, eyes, mouth and brain.

A is wrong: In utero infection is rare.

C is wrong: Breast milk is not the main route.

D is wrong: Ultrasound does not transmit infection.

177. A pregnant client in Davao keeps cats at home. Which teaching helps prevent toxoplasmosis?

A. Avoid cat feces, cook food at appropriate temperatures and wash vegetables well

B. Give the cats a rabies vaccine every month

C. Avoid all contact with dogs

D. Drink only boiled water and avoid all fruits

Answer: A. Avoid cat feces, cook food at appropriate temperatures and wash vegetables well

Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infection spread by cat feces and undercooked meat or unwashed produce. Interventions are to avoid cat feces (someone else changes the litter box or she wears gloves and washes hands), cook food thoroughly and wash fruits and vegetables. Infection can cause fetal eye, brain and growth problems.

B is wrong: Rabies vaccination of cats does not prevent toxoplasmosis.

C is wrong: Dogs do not transmit toxoplasma.

D is wrong: Fruits are healthy if washed, and boiled water does not address the main sources.

178. A primigravida at 8 weeks tells the nurse she is happy about the pregnancy but also worried and sometimes wishes she were not pregnant. What is the best response?

A. Refer her immediately for psychiatric evaluation

B. Acknowledge that mixed feelings are normal in the first trimester

C. Tell her she should not feel that way

D. Advise her to stop thinking about it until delivery

Answer: B. Acknowledge that mixed feelings are normal in the first trimester

Ambivalence, feeling both joy and doubt, is a normal psychological response in the first trimester and should be acknowledged as normal. It usually fades as the pregnancy becomes real, often when the fetus is felt to move. The nurse listens, normalizes feelings and monitors for persistent depression or thoughts of self-harm.

A is wrong: Psychiatric referral is not needed for typical ambivalence.

C is wrong: Dismissing feelings is non-therapeutic and invalidates her.

D is wrong: Avoiding the topic does not help her adjust.

179. A client on day 3 after normal delivery in a lying-in clinic is tearful, irritable and anxious but cares for her baby. Which is the best nursing response?

A. Start antidepressant medication immediately

B. Offer reassurance, rest and emotional support because this is expected and self-limiting

C. Report her to social services for neglect

D. Separate her from the baby to let her rest

Answer: B. Offer reassurance, rest and emotional support because this is expected and self-limiting

Postpartum blues affect up to 80 percent of new mothers, start about 2 to 3 days after delivery and last up to 2 weeks. They are self-limiting and managed with reassurance, rest, family support and a chance to talk. She is still caring for her baby, so no neglect is present. Reassess if symptoms continue beyond 2 weeks.

A is wrong: Medication is not needed for self-limiting blues.

C is wrong: She is caring for the baby, so no neglect is seen.

D is wrong: Separation interferes with bonding and rooming-in.

180. A woman 5 weeks postpartum reports persistent sadness, loss of interest, poor appetite and difficulty bonding with her baby. Which condition does this suggest?

A. Postpartum depression

B. Postpartum blues

C. Postpartum psychosis

D. Normal adjustment

Answer: A. Postpartum depression

Postpartum depression is longer-lasting and more severe than the blues. Symptoms such as persistent sadness, anhedonia, appetite and sleep changes and poor bonding last more than 2 weeks and impair function. It needs referral, counseling and often medication, and a screening tool is used. Always ask about thoughts of harming herself or the baby.

B is wrong: Blues resolve within about 2 weeks.

C is wrong: Psychosis involves delusions, hallucinations and loss of reality.

D is wrong: Five weeks of marked symptoms exceeds a normal adjustment.

181. A woman 10 days postpartum is brought to the health center because she hears voices telling her to harm the baby. What is the priority?

A. Ensure the safety of the infant and mother and arrange emergency psychiatric care

B. Reassure her that this is common postpartum blues

C. Schedule outpatient counseling next month

D. Teach relaxation breathing

Answer: A. Ensure the safety of the infant and mother and arrange emergency psychiatric care

Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with hallucinations, delusions, confusion and risk of suicide or infanticide. The infant and mother must be kept safe, with the baby not left alone with her, and urgent psychiatric evaluation and admission arranged. Hearing commands to harm the baby is the red flag. Safety comes first.

B is wrong: Blues do not involve hallucinations or commands to harm.

C is wrong: Delaying care for a month risks harm to the baby.

D is wrong: Relaxation alone does not address psychosis.

182. Which finding differentiates postpartum depression from postpartum blues?

A. Crying spells beginning on the third day

B. Mood swings that improve with rest

C. Occurrence in about 80 percent of new mothers

D. Symptoms that last longer than 2 weeks and impair daily functioning

Answer: D. Symptoms that last longer than 2 weeks and impair daily functioning

Blues begin 2 to 3 days after delivery, affect about 80 percent of mothers and resolve on their own within about 2 weeks. Postpartum depression persists longer than 2 weeks, is more intense and interferes with caring for self and baby. The duration and severity make the difference. Remember: blues pass, depression stays.

A is wrong: Early crying spells are typical for blues.

B is wrong: Improvement with rest fits the blues.

C is wrong: The high frequency of 80 percent applies to blues.

183. Which instruction about vaginal bleeding should the nurse give a client being discharged after hysterectomy?

A. Bleeding as heavy as menstruation is expected during the first week

B. Any spotting at all must be reported immediately

C. Soaking pads for two weeks is normal

D. Light spotting may last up to 6 weeks, but bleeding as heavy as a menstrual flow should be reported

Answer: D. Light spotting may last up to 6 weeks, but bleeding as heavy as a menstrual flow should be reported

After hysterectomy, a client may have light spotting for up to 6 weeks. Bleeding as heavy as a menstrual flow signals hemorrhage and must be reported, along with fever, foul discharge or severe pain. She also receives pain medication and a short hospital stay of 1 to 2 days. Teach her warning signs before discharge.

A is wrong: Menstrual-strength bleeding is abnormal and needs reporting.

B is wrong: Light spotting is normal during recovery.

C is wrong: Soaked pads indicate heavy bleeding that needs evaluation.

184. When may a woman resume heavy lifting and sexual intercourse after a hysterectomy?

A. After 1 week

B. After about 6 weeks, with the surgeon's clearance

C. After 2 weeks

D. Immediately when the pain subsides

Answer: B. After about 6 weeks, with the surgeon's clearance

After hysterectomy the client may resume sexual activity, heavy lifting and usual activities after about 6 weeks, when internal healing, especially of the vaginal cuff, is complete. Early activity risks bleeding and wound or cuff dehiscence. Walking is encouraged earlier to prevent clots. Confirm with the surgeon at the follow-up visit.

A is wrong: One week is too early for tissue healing.

C is wrong: Two weeks is still too early for lifting and intercourse.

D is wrong: Pain relief from medication does not mean tissues have healed.

185. A client in a Cebu hospital asks what to expect after hysterectomy. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

A. Your periods will continue but be lighter

B. You will no longer need any gynecologic follow-up

C. Your hospital stay will last about 3 weeks

D. You will no longer have periods, but ask your doctor about continued cervical cancer screening

Answer: D. You will no longer have periods, but ask your doctor about continued cervical cancer screening

After hysterectomy the client no longer menstruates, but the review notes she may still be at risk for cervical cancer, so she should ask about continued screening, especially if the cervix was kept or if the surgery was for cancer. The hospital stay is usually only 1 to 2 days, and follow-up is still needed. Teach her to report heavy bleeding.

A is wrong: Without a uterus, menstruation stops.

B is wrong: Follow-up and screening may still be needed.

C is wrong: Stay is usually 1 to 2 days, not 3 weeks.

186. Four pregnant women arrive at a Quezon City emergency room at the same time. Which client should the nurse see first?

A. A woman with stable light bleeding and normal vital signs

B. A woman who just had a seizure and has BP 170/112

C. A woman with a small laceration on the forearm

D. A woman in early latent labor with mild contractions

Answer: B. A woman who just had a seizure and has BP 170/112

Triage in pregnant clients places seizure or eclampsia in the immediate category because airway, aspiration and fetal oxygenation are threatened. Stable bleeding and minor lacerations are urgent or less urgent. Use airway, breathing, circulation and life threat to rank. Eclampsia means ABCs and magnesium sulfate now.

A is wrong: Stable bleeding with normal vital signs can wait briefly.

C is wrong: A minor laceration is not life-threatening.

D is wrong: Early latent labor is non-urgent.

187. A pregnant woman at 28 weeks with heavy active vaginal bleeding and a woman at 30 weeks with stable minimal spotting arrive together. How should the nurse triage them?

A. See both at the same time

B. See the woman with active heavy bleeding first, and the stable woman next

C. See the woman with spotting first because she is further along

D. Send the woman with heavy bleeding to the waiting area

Answer: B. See the woman with active heavy bleeding first, and the stable woman next

Pregnant women with active bleeding are an emergent priority because of risk of hemorrhagic shock and fetal compromise, while stable bleeding is urgent. The nurse assesses bleeding amount, vital signs and fetal heart tones, starts IV access and avoids vaginal examination until previa is excluded. Priority rises with instability.

A is wrong: Splitting attention delays the unstable client.

C is wrong: Gestational age does not decide priority here.

D is wrong: Active heavy bleeding must not wait.

188. A pregnant client smokes 10 sticks of cigarettes daily. Which fetal effect should the nurse emphasize in teaching?

A. Increased birth weight from nicotine

B. Reduced oxygen delivery leading to growth restriction and low birth weight

C. Neural tube defects only

D. Prolonged gestation with macrosomia

Answer: B. Reduced oxygen delivery leading to growth restriction and low birth weight

Smoking during pregnancy affects the baby. Nicotine and carbon monoxide constrict placental vessels and reduce oxygen delivery, causing intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight, preterm birth and higher risk of stillbirth and placental problems. Encourage cessation at any stage and offer counseling resources. Think smoke equals small baby.

A is wrong: Smoking lowers birth weight, it does not raise it.

C is wrong: Neural tube defects are linked to folate deficiency.

D is wrong: Smoking is linked to preterm birth, not macrosomia.

189. A pregnant client tells the nurse she drinks alcohol regularly. Which condition puts the baby at risk?

A. Hemolytic disease of the newborn

B. Congenital hypothyroidism

C. Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders

D. Cystic fibrosis

Answer: C. Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders

Drinking alcohol during pregnancy can lead to fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, with growth restriction, characteristic facial features, and brain and behavior problems. No safe amount has been established, so women are advised to abstain. Brain development continues throughout pregnancy, so stopping at any time helps.

A is wrong: Hemolytic disease relates to blood group incompatibility.

B is wrong: Congenital hypothyroidism is a thyroid problem unrelated to alcohol.

D is wrong: Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder.

190. A newborn of a mother who used opioids during pregnancy is irritable with a high-pitched cry and tremors. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

A. Hypoglycemia from maternal diabetes

B. Congenital rubella

C. Neonatal withdrawal (abstinence) syndrome

D. Physiologic jaundice

Answer: C. Neonatal withdrawal (abstinence) syndrome

Use of illegal drugs in pregnancy can lead to developmental problems and neonatal withdrawal symptoms such as irritability, high-pitched cry, tremors, poor feeding, sweating and diarrhea. Care includes a quiet environment, swaddling, small frequent feedings and scoring with a withdrawal tool, with medication if severe. Observe the baby for several days.

A is wrong: Hypoglycemia relates to diabetic mothers and is not drug withdrawal.

B is wrong: Congenital rubella gives cataract, deafness and heart defects.

D is wrong: Physiologic jaundice is a skin color change after 24 hours.

191. A pregnant client at 8 weeks drinks four cups of brewed coffee a day. What should the nurse advise?

A. Caffeine is completely safe in any amount

B. Switch to energy drinks

C. Increase intake to stay alert

D. Limit caffeine to less than 200 mg a day because high intake in the first trimester raises miscarriage risk

Answer: D. Limit caffeine to less than 200 mg a day because high intake in the first trimester raises miscarriage risk

Caffeine in the first trimester can increase the risk of miscarriage, so intake should be limited to less than 200 mg per day, about one or two small cups of coffee. Four cups is well over the limit. Tea, soft drinks, chocolate and energy drinks also contain caffeine, so count all sources. Remember: first trimester caffeine, less than 200 mg a day, which is roughly one 12 ounce cup of brewed coffee.

A is wrong: Large intake is not safe in early pregnancy.

B is wrong: Energy drinks have high caffeine and other stimulants.

C is wrong: Increasing intake raises the risk further.

192. Which advice about canned tuna is appropriate for a pregnant woman?

A. Eat it daily as the main protein source

B. Avoid all fish, including sardines and tilapia

C. Eat it raw to preserve nutrients

D. Eat it in moderation because it contains mercury

Answer: D. Eat it in moderation because it contains mercury

Canned tuna contains mercury, which can harm the developing fetal nervous system, so it should be taken in moderation. Fish low in mercury such as sardines, tilapia and bangus are good sources of protein and omega-3 fats. Large predator fish such as shark and swordfish should be avoided. Raw fish carries infection risk.

A is wrong: Daily intake can accumulate mercury.

B is wrong: Low-mercury fish are beneficial and need not be avoided.

C is wrong: Raw fish risks bacterial and parasitic infection.

193. Which finding is a maternal indication for cesarean birth?

A. Previous low transverse cesarean incision

B. Gestational diabetes with normal fetal size

C. Active genital herpes lesions

D. Mild anemia

Answer: C. Active genital herpes lesions

Primary maternal indications for cesarean birth include cephalopelvic disproportion, active genital herpes lesions, a previous classical incision and severe preeclampsia or eclampsia. Active herpes lesions in labor risk neonatal infection during vaginal delivery. A previous low transverse incision allows a trial of labor, and GDM or mild anemia alone are not indications.

A is wrong: A low transverse scar usually permits a vaginal birth after cesarean.

B is wrong: Well-controlled GDM with normal fetal size does not require cesarean.

D is wrong: Mild anemia alone is not an indication.

194. A client in labor has a loop of umbilical cord visible at the vaginal opening and the fetal heart rate is dropping. This fetal condition is a primary indication for which procedure?

A. Emergency cesarean birth

B. Amniotomy

C. Oxytocin augmentation

D. Vacuum extraction at high station

Answer: A. Emergency cesarean birth

Prolapsed umbilical cord is a fetal indication for cesarean birth, along with fetal distress and malpresentations. Meanwhile the nurse relieves pressure by placing the client in knee-chest or Trendelenburg position and pushing the presenting part upward with a gloved hand, covering the cord with moist saline gauze and giving oxygen. Cord compression causes fetal hypoxia.

B is wrong: Amniotomy would worsen the prolapse.

C is wrong: Oxytocin increases contractions and cord compression.

D is wrong: Vacuum extraction at high station is unsafe and slow.

195. Which placental condition is a primary indication for cesarean birth?

A. Posterior placenta

B. Anterior fundal placenta

C. Mildly calcified placenta at 39 weeks

D. Complete placenta previa

Answer: D. Complete placenta previa

Placental indications for cesarean birth are placenta previa and abruptio placentae with maternal or fetal compromise. In complete previa the placenta covers the cervical os, so vaginal delivery would cause severe hemorrhage. Placenta location in the fundus or posterior wall is normal and does not interfere with birth.

A is wrong: A posterior placenta is a normal location.

B is wrong: An anterior fundal placenta is also normal.

C is wrong: Calcification near term is a normal aging change.

196. Which pre-operative action is required before an emergency cesarean birth?

A. Insert a nasogastric tube and give a full meal

B. Perform a vaginal examination for dilation

C. Give an oral laxative

D. Insert a retention catheter and keep the client strictly NPO

Answer: D. Insert a retention catheter and keep the client strictly NPO

Before cesarean birth, a retention (Foley) catheter keeps the bladder empty and away from the surgical field, and strict NPO status lowers the risk of aspiration during anesthesia. Fetal heart rate is monitored continuously until right before abdominal prep. Consent, labs, IV access and antibiotics are also prepared.

A is wrong: Feeding before surgery raises aspiration risk.

B is wrong: A vaginal examination is not required and may add infection risk.

C is wrong: Laxatives are not part of urgent surgical preparation.

197. Where should the nurse place a wedge or rolled towel for a client before cesarean section?

A. Under the right hip to tilt the uterus to the left

B. Under the left hip to tilt the uterus to the right

C. Under the head to elevate it

D. Under the knees only

Answer: A. Under the right hip to tilt the uterus to the left

A wedge or rolled towel under the mother's right hip displaces the uterus to the left and prevents compression of the inferior vena cava and aorta. This avoids supine hypotensive syndrome, which reduces maternal blood pressure and uteroplacental perfusion. Keep the tilt during transport and surgery until the baby is delivered.

B is wrong: A left hip wedge would shift the uterus toward the vena cava.

C is wrong: Raising the head does not relieve vena cava compression.

D is wrong: Knee support does not displace the uterus.

198. Until when should the nurse continue to monitor the fetal heart rate before a cesarean section?

A. Until the consent form is signed

B. Continuously until right before abdominal preparation is done

C. Every 4 hours only

D. Only after the incision is made
